Carbonic acid, forming sodium bicarbonate
questions.explanation: The sequence: CO2 + H2O makes H2CO3; H2CO3 + 2NaOH makes Na2CO3 + 2H2O (the most common reaction); then Na2CO3 + Ca(OH)2 makes CaCO3 + 2NaOH. The instructor said to expect this as a board question in the form 'what does X react with to form Y.'
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 3 (PDF p. 2)
questions.disc: Slide 3 prints calcium hydroxide as Ca(OH). The correct formula is Ca(OH)2, which is what this question uses.

questions.stem: What produces the small oscillations on this capnogram?
options: Spontaneous breaths against the ventilator
Contraction of the heart and great vessels
A cuff leak around the endotracheal tube
Exhausted CO2 absorbent
questions.explanation: These are cardiac oscillations, caused by contraction of the heart and great vessels moving small volumes of gas. A curare cleft (a dip in the plateau) signals spontaneous effort against the ventilator; an exhausted absorbent raises the baseline; a leak slopes the trace.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 47 (PDF p. 48)

questions.stem: Why may SpO2 differ from the SaO2 reported by the lab when abnormal hemoglobins are present?
options: SpO2 estimates arterial PaO2 rather than hemoglobin saturation
SpO2 includes carboxyhemoglobin in its denominator by design
The lab analyzer reports venous rather than arterial saturation
SpO2 reports functional saturation; the lab co-oximeter reports fractional saturation
questions.explanation: Pulse oximetry measures functional saturation using two wavelengths. Lab co-oximetry uses multiple wavelengths and reports fractional saturation, accounting for other hemoglobins. When those are present, SpO2 may not match the lab SaO2.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 75 (PDF p. 76)

questions.stem: Midway through a case, the N2O E-cylinder gauge reads 745 psig. What can you conclude about the remaining contents?
options: Liquid N2O remains, but the gauge can't show how much; weigh the cylinder
The cylinder is essentially full, holding about 1590 L of N2O
The cylinder is about half full, since pressure falls linearly with use
The liquid phase is gone and only gaseous N2O remains
questions.explanation: N2O's critical temperature is about 36 C, so at room temperature it stays liquid under pressure. Liquid and gas sit in equilibrium and the gauge holds at 745 psig until the last liquid vaporizes. Anything from full to nearly empty can read 745, which is why the instructor noted you have to weigh the cylinder. The linear pressure-volume rule applies to O2 and air, not N2O.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 14 (PDF p. 7)

questions.stem: How does a copper kettle vaporizer differ from a variable bypass vaporizer?
options: It heats and pressurizes the agent to 2 atm like the Tec 6
It uses a bimetallic strip to adjust its splitting ratio
It uses wicks and baffles, so the dial reads true concentration
It isn't calibrated for concentration, so output must be calculated
questions.explanation: In a copper kettle, a dedicated O2 flow is bubbled through liquid agent to make saturated vapor, which then joins the main fresh gas. Copper conducts heat well and keeps temperature stable, but the device isn't concentration-calibrated, so calculations are required. Wicks, baffles, and bimetallic strips belong to the variable bypass design; heat and pressure belong to the Tec 6.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 74 (PDF p. 37)

questions.stem: Which conditions increase ETCO2 by raising CO2 production? Select 3.
options: Pulmonary embolism
Seizures
Fever
Sepsis
Hypothermia
Hypothyroidism
questions.explanation: Increased metabolic rate raises CO2 production: fever or hyperthermia, sepsis, seizures, MH, shivering, and hyperthyroidism. Hypothermia and hypothyroidism lower production. PE lowers ETCO2 by cutting CO2 delivery to the lungs.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slides 43, 51 (PDF p. 43, 52)

questions.stem: Which events can deliver a hypoxic mixture despite a working fail-safe valve and proportioning system? Select 3.
options: Nitrogen contamination of the O2 pipeline
N2O set at 4 L/min with O2 turned to 0.5 L/min
A cracked O2 flowmeter tube
O2 supply pressure falling to 20 psig with N2O on
Hanging an N2O cylinder on the O2 yoke
Crossed O2 and N2O pipelines
questions.explanation: Both safety systems sense only pressure, not O2 itself, so crossed pipelines and nitrogen contamination slip past them (the lecture cites real events from 2024 and 2019). A cracked flowmeter tube leaks O2 downstream of both. Low O2 supply pressure triggers the fail-safe, a low O2 to N2O ratio triggers the proportioner, and PISS prevents an N2O cylinder from fitting the O2 yoke.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slides 46, 48 (PDF p. 23, 24)

questions.stem: By definition, when is soda lime exhausted?
options: When all the hydroxides have become carbonates
When the indicator turns fully purple
When it stops producing heat
When all of its water has evaporated
questions.explanation: Exhaustion occurs when all hydroxides have been converted to carbonates. Color change is only a rough guide and isn't to be relied on, because the dye can regenerate and channeling can mislead.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 2 (PDF p. 1)

questions.stem: A vaporizer must be removed from the manifold and carried to another room. Which setting prevents agent leakage during the move?
options: Transport (T) mode
The zero (off) position
The interlock release position
The highest dial setting
questions.explanation: T (transport) mode secures the vaporizer to prevent leakage. The lecture's intervention for tipping is to avoid moving a vaporizer that isn't in transport mode, because tipping sends liquid into the bypass chamber. The interlock (push button, turn counterclockwise) controls turning it on.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slides 59, 64 (PDF p. 30, 32)

questions.stem: A spontaneously breathing patient under sedation has significant metabolic acidosis. How would you expect ETCO2 to change?
options: No change, since metabolic disorders don't affect ETCO2
Increase, from higher CO2 production
Decrease, from compensatory hyperventilation
Increase, from compensatory hypoventilation
questions.explanation: Box 18.1 lists metabolic acidosis (if spontaneously breathing) under hyperventilation, which lowers ETCO2. Metabolic alkalosis in a spontaneously breathing patient causes hypoventilation and raises ETCO2.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 43 (PDF p. 43)

questions.stem: A patient receives a pure TIVA with an ETT. Which statement about gas monitoring is correct?
options: Expired agent monitoring detects propofol concentration
ETCO2 is still required even though expired agent readings aren't useful
The infrared analyzer can't read CO2 unless a volatile is present
Capnography can be omitted because no volatile agent is given
questions.explanation: With pure TIVA there's no gas in and no gas out, so expired agent monitoring doesn't matter, but ETCO2 is still required. Infrared analysis measures CO2 independently of any volatile. There are no contraindications to capnography interpreted in clinical context.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 48 (PDF p. 49)

questions.stem: A small leak exists in the low-pressure breathing circuit. Which change makes the leak (and room contamination) worse?
options: Using the pause fresh gas flow function
Nothing; effective scavenging captures leaked gas
Lower peak circuit pressure
Higher peak circuit pressure
questions.explanation: There's a direct linear relationship between peak circuit pressure and gas escaping through a low-pressure leak: higher pressure, bigger leak. Scavenging only captures gas leaving through the relief valves, so even with effective scavenging up to 2 L/min can leak, raising room N2O by 100-200 ppm.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 13 (PDF p. 7)

questions.stem: A cold, vasoconstricted patient's pulse oximeter intermittently shows no reading. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Hypothermia and low perfusion limit the device's ability to calculate SpO2
The oximeter needs recalibration to room air (21%)
Venous pulsation is being mistaken for arterial flow
The probe's 660 nm LED fails at low skin temperature
questions.explanation: Motion, low perfusion, hypothermia, dyes, nail polish, ambient light, electrocautery, and infrared systems can impair oximetry. Extreme hypothermia or hypoperfusion can prevent the device from finding enough pulsatile signal to calculate SpO2. Pulse oximeters are autocalibrating.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 78 (PDF p. 79)

questions.stem: Which US cylinder color codes are correct? Select 3.
options: Carbon dioxide: brown
Helium: gray
Medical air: yellow
Medical air: black
Nitrous oxide: blue
Oxygen: green
questions.explanation: US colors: O2 green, N2O blue, air yellow, CO2 gray, helium brown. Nitrogen is black. CO2 and helium are the easy ones to swap.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 7 (PDF p. 4)

questions.stem: A fire breaks out in one OR suite. Which pipeline component lets staff shut off gas to that area without cutting supply to the rest of the hospital?
options: Pipeline inlet check valve
Zone valve
DISS connector
Line pressure regulator
questions.explanation: Zone valves isolate areas of the pipeline for maintenance or emergencies. Line pressure regulators reduce pressure, check valves prevent backflow at the machine inlet, and DISS prevents misconnection.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 28 (PDF p. 14)

questions.stem: On this normal capnogram, which segment represents alveolar gas being sampled?
options: A to B
B to C
C to D
D to E
questions.explanation: A to B is anatomic dead space with essentially no CO2. B to C is the expiratory upstroke as CO2-containing gas arrives. C to D is the alveolar (expiratory) plateau, when alveolar gas is sampled. D is ETCO2, the best reflection of alveolar CO2. D to E is the inspiratory downstroke as fresh gas is entrained.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 44 (PDF p. 44)

questions.stem: Using the lecture's property table, which lists blood:gas partition coefficients from lowest to highest?
options: N2O, desflurane, sevoflurane, halothane, isoflurane
Desflurane, N2O, sevoflurane, isoflurane, halothane
Desflurane, sevoflurane, N2O, isoflurane, halothane
Sevoflurane, desflurane, N2O, isoflurane, halothane
questions.explanation: Blood:gas values: des 0.42, N2O 0.46, sevo 0.65, iso 1.46, halothane 2.5. Des and N2O are close, but des is lowest, which is why it has the fastest onset and recovery.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 50 (PDF p. 25)

questions.stem: What does The Joint Commission require regarding waste anesthetic gases?
options: Passive scavenging is acceptable in all ORs
All WAGs must be scavenged using active methods
WAG levels must be measured before every case
Scavenging is required only when N2O is used
questions.explanation: TJC requires that all WAGs be scavenged using active scavenging methods. A working scavenging system reduces trace gas concentrations by about 90%. Instructor note: TJC requires WAG scavenging.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 18 (PDF p. 9)

questions.stem: A traditional Thorpe tube flowmeter is best described as:
options: Variable pressure, variable orifice
Constant pressure, constant orifice
Variable pressure, constant orifice
Constant pressure, variable orifice
questions.explanation: As flow rises, the float climbs the tapered tube and the annular space (orifice) gets larger, while the pressure drop across the float stays constant. Flow is read at the widest part of the indicator.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slides 42, 43 (PDF p. 21, 22)

questions.stem: Which statements about standard pulse oximeter operation are correct? Select 2.
options: It measures tissue O2 delivery at the probe site
It must be manually calibrated to room air before each case
It distinguishes COHb from oxyhemoglobin with a third wavelength
Plethysmography separates the pulsatile arterial signal from venous and tissue absorption
It uses red light near 660 nm and infrared near 940 nm
It reports fractional saturation, the same as a lab co-oximeter
questions.explanation: Two LEDs (660 nm red, 940 nm IR) and the Beer-Lambert law let the device estimate SpO2 from the ratio of absorbance; plethysmography isolates the pulsatile arterial component. SpO2 is FUNCTIONAL saturation, the device is autocalibrating, it can't distinguish COHb, and it doesn't measure tissue O2 delivery.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slides 74, 75 (PDF p. 75, 76)

questions.stem: What is the maximum dial setting on a sevoflurane variable bypass vaporizer?
questions.explanation: Variable bypass vaporizers are calibrated per agent: sevo up to 8%, other agents up to 5%. The des vaporizer goes to 12% or higher.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slides 58, 64 (PDF p. 29, 32)

questions.stem: Which problems can cause inaccurate flowmeter readings? Select 3.
options: Debris in the flowmeter tube
Static electricity in the tube
A sticking indicator float
Turbulent flow at high flow rates
Reading the float at its widest part
Laminar flow at low flow rates
questions.explanation: Inaccurate flow comes from debris, indicator sticking, indicator misalignment, and static electricity. Reading the widest part of the indicator is the correct technique, and laminar flow at low rates and turbulent flow at high rates are normal flowmeter physics built into each tube's calibration.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 47 (PDF p. 24)

questions.stem: How should a nasopharyngeal airway be prepared for insertion, and where does it end up?
options: Water-based lubricant; tip advanced into the trachea
No lubricant needed; tip positioned at the vocal cords
Water-based lubricant or local anesthetic; tip in the hypopharynx
Petroleum-based jelly; tip resting in the oropharynx
questions.explanation: NPAs are inserted with water-based lubricant or local anesthetic, and they lie in the hypopharynx. They're better tolerated than OPAs in awake patients; the most common complication is epistaxis.
questions.citation: Airway Equipment (McPherson): slide 6 (PDF p. 6)

questions.stem: Which feature lets an open-reservoir scavenging interface work without pressure relief valves?
options: The ventilator's pressure relief valve
Relief ports open to the atmosphere
A reservoir bag that collapses when vacuum is excessive
Spring-loaded pop-off and pop-in valves
questions.explanation: The open interface is valveless; relief ports open to atmosphere keep positive or negative pressure from building up, so it doesn't depend on relief valves working properly. Instructor note: the open interface is most common. Pop-off and pop-in valves belong to the closed interface.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 20 (PDF p. 10)

questions.stem: What does the lecture say about the traditional Allen test before radial cannulation?
options: It replaces ultrasound when pulses are weak
It has not been confirmed as a reliable test
It is required before every radial arterial line
It reliably predicts hand ischemia after cannulation
questions.explanation: Slide 66 states the traditional Allen test hasn't been confirmed as reliable; ultrasound with Doppler improves cannulation when pulses are weak or vessels small. Slide 68 still mentions assessing ulnar circulation, so know that both statements appear, but the reliability point is the one to remember.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slides 66, 68 (PDF p. 67, 69)

questions.stem: Which are among the four parts of a typical waste gas scavenging system? Select 3.
options: CO2 absorber canister
Disposal line
Inspiratory unidirectional valve
Breathing circuit reservoir bag
Relief valve where gas leaves the breathing circuit
Scavenging interface
questions.explanation: The four parts: (1) a relief valve (APL or ventilator relief), (2) conducting tubing to the interface, (3) the scavenging interface, and (4) a disposal line. The absorber, unidirectional valves, and patient reservoir bag belong to the breathing circuit.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 18 (PDF p. 9)

questions.stem: Which numbered component minimizes the vaporizer pumping effect from positive pressure ventilation and O2 flush use?
options: Component 2
Component 3
Component 4
Component 5
questions.explanation: Component 5 is the outlet check valve between the vaporizers and the common gas outlet. It blocks retrograde pressure from the circuit, which minimizes pumping. Component 4 is the pressure relief valve, and 2 and 3 are the second-stage regulators.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slides 5, 72 (PDF p. 3, 36)

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a high-volume, low-pressure cuff on an endotracheal tube?
options: Seal the airway with a very small cuff volume
Keep cuff pressure high to prevent any leak
Spread cuff force over a larger area of tracheal wall
Seal with high pressure over a small contact area
questions.explanation: High-volume, low-pressure cuffs disperse the sealing force across a larger area of tracheal tissue. The distractors describe the opposite design: high pressure concentrated on a small area of mucosa.
questions.citation: Airway Equipment (McPherson): slide 7 (PDF p. 7)

questions.stem: Under ASA Standard 2.4, when must body temperature be monitored?
options: During every anesthetic lasting longer than 30 minutes in total
Only when forced-air or other active warming devices are used
Only during general anesthesia when volatile agents are used
When significant temperature changes are intended, anticipated, or suspected
questions.explanation: The standard: every patient shall have temperature monitored when clinically significant changes in body temperature are intended, anticipated, or suspected. The objective is maintaining appropriate body temperature.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 14 (PDF p. 14)

questions.stem: Shortly after intubation, the ventilator displays this pressure-volume loop. Which problem best explains its shape?
options: Increased airway resistance during inspiration, as in a bitten ETT
A leak in the breathing circuit
Abnormally increased compliance, as in emphysema
Increased airway resistance during expiration, as in bronchospasm
questions.explanation: The loop is closed but widened, with the expiratory limb bowed out, the lecture's pattern for increased resistance on expiration (bronchospasm). A kinked or bitten ETT bows the inspiratory limb. A leak leaves the loop open, and increased compliance makes it tall and steep toward the volume axis.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 29 (PDF p. 29)

questions.stem: Which statements about NIOSH and OSHA are correct? Select 2.
options: OSHA enacts and enforces standards and recommends scavenging in all anesthetizing locations
NIOSH sets a 25 ppm limit for halogenated agents
NIOSH enforces its 2 ppm limit through OR inspections
NIOSH researches exposure hazards and recommends standards
OSHA requires active scavenging by accreditation survey
OSHA conducts the research and NIOSH enforces the law
questions.explanation: The 1970 Occupational Safety and Health Act created NIOSH (research and recommended standards) and OSHA (enacts and enforces them, and recommends scavenging in all anesthetizing locations). NIOSH limits: halogenated agents alone 2 ppm, N2O alone 25 ppm. The active-scavenging requirement comes from TJC, not OSHA.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slides 9, 10 (PDF p. 5)
questions.supp: NIOSH's 1977 recommendation also covers combined use: when halogenated agents are given WITH N2O, the halogenated limit drops from 2 ppm to 0.5 ppm (ceiling over a sampling period up to 1 hour), and N2O stays at 25 ppm TWA. Slide 10 lists only the 2 ppm and 25 ppm values.

questions.stem: Why does N2O exist as a liquid in an E-cylinder at room temperature while O2 remains a gas?
options: N2O's boiling point is above room temperature, while O2's boiling point is below
N2O's critical temp (about 36 C) is above room temp; O2's (-118.6 C) is far below
O2's critical temp is above room temp, but it's filled below its liquefying pressure
N2O is filled to a much higher pressure than O2 is in an E-cylinder
questions.explanation: A gas can only be liquefied by pressure below its critical temperature. N2O's critical temperature (about 36 C) is above room temperature, so compressing it liquefies it. O2's is -118.6 C, the highest temperature at which O2 can exist as a liquid, so no pressure will liquefy it at room temperature. N2O's boiling point is -88 C, and its fill pressure (745 psig) is lower than O2's.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slides 11, 14 (PDF p. 6, 7)

questions.stem: Where is the O2 fail-safe valve located, and what does it sense?
options: In the O2 supply line; it senses N2O supply pressure
In the N2O supply line; it senses inspired O2 concentration
In the O2 supply line; it senses O2 flow at the flowmeter
In the N2O supply line; it senses O2 supply pressure
questions.explanation: Instructor note: it sits in the nitrous line but responds to O2 pressure. When O2 supply pressure falls below about 25-30 psig it reduces, and below about 20 psig stops, the flow of other gases. It never measures concentration, so it can't catch the wrong gas in the O2 line.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 34 (PDF p. 17)

questions.stem: A sidestream capnography line keeps occluding with condensation during a long case. Which measure does the lecture suggest?
options: Move the sampling port to the expiratory limb of the absorber
Elevate the sampling line above the circuit and use humidity barriers
Lower the sampling line below the patient to drain water
Increase the sampling rate to clear the line
questions.explanation: Sampling lines and water traps can occlude with condensation. Elevating the sampling line above the circuit reduces water entry, and humidity barriers reduce condensation. Higher sampling rates can falsely lower ETCO2, especially in small patients.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 49 (PDF p. 50)

questions.stem: The alveolar plateau (phase C to D) develops a noticeable upward slope. What does this indicate?
options: Rebreathing of CO2
Esophageal intubation
Ventilation-perfusion mismatch
Spontaneous breathing against the ventilator
questions.explanation: Normally phase C to D is nearly horizontal. When ventilation and perfusion are mismatched, it slopes upward as alveoli with different CO2 levels empty at different times. Rebreathing raises the baseline, and spontaneous effort causes a cleft.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 44 (PDF p. 44)

questions.stem: Which safety feature is designed specifically to prevent filling a vaporizer with the wrong agent?
options: Temperature-compensating bimetallic strip
Outlet check valve downstream of the vaporizer
Agent-specific key fill system matching bottle to vaporizer
Vaporizer interlock allowing only one dial on at a time
questions.explanation: The key fill system matches the bottle adapter to the vaporizer, along with agent-specific color coding. The lecture's intervention: always double-check that the correct bottle, key, and vaporizer are used. The interlock prevents turning on more than one vaporizer; it doesn't stop misfilling.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slides 59, 70 (PDF p. 30, 35)

questions.stem: Following the lecture's pre-induction sequence, which is placed first?
options: Pulse oximeter, to record SpO2 on room air
NIBP cuff, to cycle a first pressure
ECG, to print a baseline strip
Face mask with 100% O2
questions.explanation: The lecture's order: SpO2 (room air reading), then preoxygenate with the mask for 3-5 minutes, then BP, then ECG with a baseline. The room-air SpO2 gives you a true baseline before supplemental O2 masks it.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 91 (PDF p. 92)

questions.stem: What role do NaOH and KOH play in soda lime?
options: They are the main CO2 absorbent, consumed before calcium hydroxide
They slow the reaction so less heat is produced
They absorb water to prevent compound A formation
They act like catalysts, speeding the initial reaction and later being regenerated
questions.explanation: NaOH and KOH react quickly with carbonic acid to form sodium and potassium carbonates. Over minutes, those carbonates react with Ca(OH)2 to form CaCO3 and water, regenerating NaOH and KOH, so they behave like catalysts. Calcium hydroxide (about 80%) is the bulk absorbent, and the reaction still produces heat.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 2 (PDF p. 1)

questions.stem: At sea level, an O2 cylinder gauge reads 1900 psig. What is the absolute pressure inside the cylinder?
options: About 1885 psia
About 1900 psia
About 1915 psia
About 1930 psia
questions.explanation: Gauge pressure is pressure above ambient: Pg = Pabs minus Patm. So Pabs = Pg + Patm = 1900 + 14.7, about 1915 psia. Subtracting 14.7 (1885) reverses the relationship.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 12 (PDF p. 6)

questions.stem: Why does moist absorbent reduce exposure to compound A during sevoflurane anesthesia?
options: Water leads to methanol formation, which breaks compound A down into low-toxicity products
Water blocks sevoflurane from contacting the hydroxides
Water warms the absorbent, which speeds compound A breakdown
Water converts compound A into carbon monoxide, which is scavenged
questions.explanation: In the presence of water, sevoflurane produces methanol, which promotes breakdown of compound A into compound B and other low-toxicity products (C, D, E). Warm, DRY absorbent promotes compound A. CO comes from the difluoromethyl ethers (des, enflurane, iso), not from compound A.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 6 (PDF p. 3)

questions.stem: The capnogram suddenly goes flat at zero. SpO2 is 99%, BP is unchanged, and PIP and exhaled tidal volume are unchanged. What is the most likely cause?
options: Cardiac arrest
Sampling line disconnection or kink
Esophageal migration of the tube
Massive pulmonary embolism
questions.explanation: Sudden waveform loss requires checking the airway, circuit, pulmonary blood flow, and sampling integrity. Stable BP rules against PE and arrest, and unchanged PIP and exhaled volume show the patient is still being ventilated through the tube. A sampling line problem is left.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slides 41, 50 (PDF p. 41, 51)

questions.stem: SpO2 keeps alarming at 88%. The provider assumes a poor probe signal and silences it without checking the patient. What does this illustrate?
options: Appropriate response to alarm fatigue
Normal practice when the waveform is noisy
Cognitive bias leading to a valid alarm being ignored
A limitation of variable-pitch alarms
questions.explanation: The lecture's example: disregarding persistent desaturation by assuming poor signal instead of true hypoxia. Cognitive bias leads clinicians to assume error instead of a real problem. Every alarm must be evaluated every time, not dismissed.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 20 (PDF p. 20)

questions.stem: According to closed-claims data, what most often causes equipment-related adverse outcomes?
options: Operator unfamiliarity or failure to verify machine function
Electrical power failure during the anesthetic
Spontaneous device malfunction or component failure
Manufacturer design defects in the anesthesia workstation
questions.explanation: Equipment-related adverse outcomes are rarely due to device malfunction. Misuse of gas delivery systems is 3x more common among claims, and operator unfamiliarity, failure to verify machine function before use, or both are the most frequent causes.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 17 (PDF p. 17)

questions.stem: Which vaporizers depend on electrical power to deliver agent? Select 2.
options: GE Aladin cassette vaporizer
Copper kettle
Variable bypass isoflurane vaporizer
Drager Vapor 3000 sevoflurane vaporizer
Tec 6 desflurane vaporizer
Variable bypass sevoflurane vaporizer
questions.explanation: The Tec 6 heats and pressurizes des and balances its circuits electronically; the lecture flags that it requires electricity. The Aladin uses a CPU, sensors, and an electronically controlled flow control valve. Variable bypass vaporizers (including the Drager Vapor 3000) and the copper kettle are mechanical.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slides 65, 66, 67 (PDF p. 33, 34)

questions.stem: Which closed-claims findings does the lecture report? Select 2.
options: Errors in judgment account for fewer than 10% of claims
Device malfunction is the leading cause of equipment-related claims
ETCO2 monitoring has no effect on esophageal intubation rates
Failure to monitor ventilation appeared in every hypoventilation claim
Distractions play no role in closed-claims events
Respiratory events are the most common preventable cause of claims and payouts
questions.explanation: Respiratory events are the most common preventable cause of claims and payouts (highlighted), and failure to monitor ventilation was identified in every hypoventilation claim. Over 65% of claims involve judgment errors, ETCO2 monitoring significantly reduces esophageal intubation, and equipment outcomes are rarely from device malfunction.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 7 (PDF p. 7)

questions.stem: Which cylinder storage practice follows the lecture's safety guidance?
options: Store empty cylinders on the machine yoke until exchange
Store cylinders on wooden racks to prevent sparks from metal contact
Store full and empty cylinders in separate areas on nonflammable racks
Store full and empty cylinders together so empties are returned quickly
questions.explanation: Full and empty cylinders go in separate areas, on nonflammable racks. Separating them prevents grabbing an empty in an emergency, and wood is a fuel source in the fire triad.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 10 (PDF p. 5)

questions.stem: A patient is in the lateral position with the NIBP cuff on the dependent arm, well below heart level. How will the readings be affected?
options: Unaffected, because oscillometry corrects for position
Falsely low
Falsely high systolic but falsely low diastolic
Falsely high
questions.explanation: A limb below heart level gives falsely high readings; a limb above the heart gives falsely low readings. The hydrostatic column between cuff and heart adds to or subtracts from the measured pressure.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slides 62, 90 (PDF p. 63, 91)

questions.stem: How does a Bourdon cylinder pressure gauge register pressure?
options: A curved flexible tube straightens under pressure and turns the needle through gears
A curved flexible tube coils tighter under pressure and turns the needle
A diaphragm compresses a calibrated spring that moves the needle
A float rises in a tapered tube in proportion to pressure
questions.explanation: The Bourdon tube is a curved, flexible tube that STRAIGHTENS when exposed to pressure; gears convert that movement into needle travel. A diaphragm and spring describe a pressure regulator, and a float in a tapered tube describes a flowmeter.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 23 (PDF p. 12)

questions.stem: How do modern clinical gas analyzers measure CO2?
options: A galvanic fuel cell consumed by CO2
Paramagnetic attraction to a magnetic field
Absorbance of red and infrared light at 660 and 940 nm
Infrared absorption, with CO2 absorbing strongly near 4.3 microns
questions.explanation: Modern analyzers use infrared absorption spectrophotometry. CO2 absorbs strongly near 4.3 microns, and multiple wavelengths also allow analysis of N2O and volatile agents. Paramagnetic and galvanic methods are O2 sensors; 660/940 nm is pulse oximetry.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 40 (PDF p. 40)

questions.stem: Which complications are associated with oropharyngeal airways? Select 3.
options: Tip passing into the hypopharynx and esophagus
Trauma to the lips and tongue
Epistaxis from nasal mucosal trauma
Stimulation of oropharyngeal and laryngeal reflexes
Vocal cord injury from the airway tip
Dental damage
questions.explanation: OPA complications: trauma to the lips and tongue, dental damage, and stimulation of oropharyngeal and laryngeal reflexes in a lightly anesthetized patient. Epistaxis is the most common NPA complication.
questions.citation: Airway Equipment (McPherson): slide 5 (PDF p. 5)

questions.stem: Which tracheal tube features are covered by the International Organization for Standardization requirements? Select 3.
options: Recommended cuff fill volume
Clinical cuff inflation pressure
Laser resistance of the shaft
Murphy eye
Internal and external diameters
Distance markers
questions.explanation: ISO requirements for tracheal tubes include ID and OD, distance markers, material toxicity, bevel, Murphy eye, and radius of curvature. Clinical cuff pressure and fill volume are use decisions, and laser resistance belongs to special laser tubes, not the general standard.
questions.citation: Airway Equipment (McPherson): slide 7 (PDF p. 7)

questions.stem: In oscillometric NIBP, which pressure corresponds to the point of maximal oscillation amplitude?
options: Diastolic pressure
Systolic pressure
Pulse pressure
Mean arterial pressure
questions.explanation: Oscillometric devices detect arterial pulsations in the cuff; MAP is associated with the maximal oscillation amplitude. Systolic and diastolic values are then estimated with device-specific algorithms, which is one reason devices vary.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 86 (PDF p. 87)

questions.stem: The 1974 findings on waste anesthetic gas exposure reported which increase among exposed MEN?
options: Cancer
Renal disease
Hepatic disease
Cataract formation
questions.explanation: Exposed women showed more spontaneous abortion, liver and kidney disease, cancer, and congenital abnormalities in offspring. Among exposed men, cancer did not increase, but hepatic disease did.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 9 (PDF p. 5)

questions.stem: During a spontaneous-ventilation mask anesthetic with sevoflurane, the O2 flush is pressed repeatedly to keep the bag full. What is the most likely consequence?
options: Agent overdose, because flush gas passes through the vaporizer
Diluted anesthetic concentration, risking a lighter plane of anesthesia
Rising ETCO2 from CO2 rebreathing through the circle system
A hypoxic mixture from gas bypassing the flowmeters entirely
questions.explanation: The flush delivers pure O2 that BYPASSES the vaporizers, so repeated use dilutes the anesthetic in the circuit (instructor note: heavily dilutes anesthetic gases). Its other listed risk is barotrauma. Pure O2 can't create a hypoxic mixture, and added fresh gas doesn't cause rebreathing.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 37 (PDF p. 19)

questions.stem: A variable bypass vaporizer delivers 1% sevoflurane at 2 L/min at 20 C, where sevo vapor is 21% of the sump gas. What is the approximate splitting ratio of bypass flow to sump inflow?
options: About 4:1
About 21:1
About 25:1
About 100:1
questions.explanation: 1% of about 2100 mL total is 21 mL of sevo vapor. Sump outflow is 21% sevo, so 79 mL of carrier gas must enter the sump to pick up 21 mL. The remaining 2000 mL bypasses. 2000:79 is about 25:1. 21:1 confuses the sump concentration with the ratio.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 55 (PDF p. 28)

questions.stem: Which spirometry loop evaluates airway resistance, and how does increased resistance change it?
options: Flow-volume loop; higher expiratory flow and a flatter loop
Flow-volume loop; lower expiratory flow and a steeper loop
Pressure-volume loop; the loop shifts toward the pressure axis
Pressure-volume loop; the loop becomes tall and steep
questions.explanation: The pressure-volume loop reflects compliance; the flow-volume loop reflects resistance. Increased resistance lowers expiratory flow and steepens the flow-volume loop (kinked or obstructed ETT, bronchospasm). A P-V loop shifting toward the pressure axis is decreased compliance, and a tall, steep P-V loop is increased compliance.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 27 (PDF p. 27)

questions.stem: What is the main advantage of a multistage over a single-stage line pressure regulator?
options: Less stable outlet pressure but higher flow capacity
Faster pressure drop when a zone valve is closed
More stable outlet pressure, because pressure is reduced in several steps
Higher outlet pressure for downstream equipment
questions.explanation: Line pressure regulators are spring-loaded valves that hold outlet pressure constant. The number of reduction steps (single vs multistage) affects pressure stability: more steps, steadier output. The goal is stability, not higher pressure.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 32 (PDF p. 16)

questions.stem: Which LMA Supreme feature allows gastric drainage?
options: Integrated bite block
Fixation tab
Drain tube
Elliptical airway tube
questions.explanation: The labeled LMA Supreme diagram shows a separate drain tube running to an opening at the cuff tip, alongside the airway tube with its 15 mm connector, an integrated bite block, a fixation tab, and a modified cuff.
questions.citation: Airway Equipment (McPherson): slide 14 (PDF p. 14)

questions.stem: A sedated patient breathing supplemental O2 becomes apneic. Which monitor will reveal the problem first?
options: Capnography
Expired anesthetic agent analysis
Pulse oximetry
Inspired O2 analyzer
questions.explanation: Pulse oximetry is a poor indicator of ventilation: a patient on supplemental O2 may be apneic for several minutes before desaturation shows up. Capnography shows loss of expired CO2 with the next missed breath. The inspired O2 analyzer measures delivered gas, and agent analysis is irrelevant without a volatile.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slides 41, 78 (PDF p. 41, 79)

questions.stem: Under volume control, PIP rises from 22 to 38 cmH2O while plateau pressure stays at 18. What is the most likely cause?
options: Bronchospasm
Endobronchial intubation
Peritoneal insufflation
Steep Trendelenburg positioning
questions.explanation: PIP reflects dynamic compliance (resistance plus compliance); plateau reflects static compliance. A rise in PIP with no change in plateau means higher airway resistance or inspiratory flow: bronchospasm, a kinked tube, secretions. Insufflation, Trendelenburg, and endobronchial intubation lower compliance and raise BOTH pressures.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slides 26, 32 (PDF p. 26, 32)

questions.stem: Sevoflurane and isoflurane vaporizers are both set to deliver 1%. Why do their splitting ratios differ?
options: The agents are metabolized to different degrees
The agents have different blood:gas coefficients
The agents have different MAC values
The agents have different vapor pressures
questions.explanation: The splitting ratio is the proportion of fresh gas bypassing vs entering the sump. Because each agent saturates the sump at a different concentration (set by its vapor pressure), the ratio needed for the same dial setting differs between agents. That's why vaporizers are agent-specific.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 54 (PDF p. 27)

questions.stem: Which agency-responsibility pairings match the lecture? Select 3.
options: CDC: medical gas cylinder labeling
DOT: employee exposure to waste gases
OSHA: anesthesia machine checkout procedures
FDA: purity and recalls of medical gases
DOT: cylinder filling, labeling, handling, and storage
ASTM: anesthesia machine component standards
questions.explanation: FDA covers gas purity, recalls, and anesthesia checkout. DOT covers manufacturing, filling, labeling, handling, and storage. The Department of Labor and CDC (OSHA, NIOSH) cover employee health and exposure. ASTM sets anesthesia machine component standards.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 4 (PDF p. 2)

questions.stem: On a normal capnogram, why does the first phase (A to B) contain essentially no CO2?
options: It is fresh gas from the inspiratory limb
It is the calibration baseline set by the monitor
It is gas from the anatomic dead space
It reflects alveolar gas from poorly perfused alveoli
questions.explanation: Phase A to B is the initial stage of expiration. Gas sampled then occupies the anatomic dead space, which doesn't take part in gas exchange, so it is normally devoid of CO2. At point B, CO2-containing gas arrives and the upstroke begins.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 44 (PDF p. 44)

questions.stem: Which sites estimate core temperature? Select 3.
options: Distal esophagus
Bladder
Mean skin temperature
Forehead skin
Fingertip skin
Nasopharynx
questions.explanation: Core temperature can be estimated from the bladder, distal esophagus, ear canal, trachea, nasopharynx, rectum, or PA blood, and core sites are preferred. Skin temperature doesn't adequately represent mean body temperature. During active cooling or rewarming, rectal temperature can lag.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slides 81, 85 (PDF p. 82, 86)

questions.stem: Gas flows preferentially along the smooth wall of a CO2 absorber canister. What is the MOST likely consequence?
options: Resistance to gas flow rises across the whole canister
The indicator changes color evenly throughout the canister
CO2 absorption improves because wall contact increases surface area
Absorbent along the flow path exhausts early while color elsewhere looks fresh
questions.explanation: Channeling is flow moving preferentially along the canister sides (between the smooth wall and irregular granules) and within the absorbent. Gas bypasses much of the absorbent, so the used path exhausts while the rest can look fresh. That's one reason color change isn't reliable. Channeling follows the path of LEAST resistance, so it doesn't raise resistance.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slides 4, 5 (PDF p. 2, 3)

questions.stem: The Eschmann introducer shown in the lecture belongs to which category of airway equipment?
options: Intubating stylet
Cricothyrotomy kit
Supraglottic airway
Nasopharyngeal airway
questions.explanation: The lecture presents the Eschmann introducer under 'Airways: Intubating Stylet.' Its images show it placed through the glottis during laryngoscopy with the ETT then loaded over it.
questions.citation: Airway Equipment (McPherson): slide 10 (PDF p. 10)

questions.stem: Compared with the aorta, how do radial artery systolic and pulse pressures usually compare?
options: They are identical when the transducer is leveled
Both are higher, because wave reflection distorts the peripheral waveform
Both are lower, because resistance falls peripherally
Systolic is lower but pulse pressure is higher
questions.explanation: As the pulse moves peripherally, wave reflection exaggerates systolic and pulse pressures, so radial SBP usually exceeds aortic SBP. The lecture also notes radial pressures can underestimate central pressures when hand vascular resistance changes, and vasodilators accentuate the discrepancy.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 70 (PDF p. 71)

questions.stem: Besides removing CO2, the absorbent conserves exhaled heat and humidity. Which change makes that effect greatest?
options: Moving the absorber to the expiratory limb
Raising fresh gas flow
Switching to a nonrebreathing circuit
Lowering fresh gas flow
questions.explanation: Exhaled heat and humidity are partially conserved by the absorbent, and both are optimized as fresh gas flow decreases, because less dry, cool fresh gas replaces the rebreathed gas. The absorber is also required for any low-flow technique.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 8 (PDF p. 4)

questions.stem: On which limbs should repeated NIBP cuff occlusion be avoided? Select 3.
options: A properly sized cuff on an obese upper arm
A limb with a fracture
An arm with a PICC line
An arm with a dialysis fistula
A lower extremity when both arms are tucked
The arm opposite a running IV
questions.explanation: Avoid repeated cuff occlusion over fractures, open injuries, dialysis fistulas, and PICC lines, and use caution after axillary node dissection. The contralateral limb is the recommended site when an IV is running, and the lower extremity is an acceptable alternative.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 89 (PDF p. 90)

questions.stem: Monday's first case is a desflurane anesthetic. The O2 flowmeter was found running at 10 L/min all weekend. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Increase fresh gas flow to wash out any CO
Proceed, because barium hydroxide lime prevents CO formation
Replace the absorbent before starting
Switch from desflurane to isoflurane
questions.explanation: High O2 flow over a weekend desiccates the absorbent, and dry absorbent with des produces the most CO (des > enflurane > iso). The recommendation is not to use absorbent known or suspected to be desiccated. Iso still produces CO, and Baralyme produces MORE CO than soda lime.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slides 6, 7 (PDF p. 3, 4)

questions.stem: Which leak is located in the machine's low-pressure system?
options: A loose vaporizer filler cap
A worn washer at the O2 cylinder yoke
A defective N2O pipeline quick connect
A leak at the first-stage regulator housing
questions.explanation: The low-pressure system runs from the flow control valves to the common gas outlet and includes flowmeters, vaporizers, check valves, and the outlet, at pressures slightly above atmospheric. A loose filler cap is a vaporizer leak that the low-pressure check may detect. Quick connects, yoke washers, and the first-stage regulator are higher-pressure parts.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slides 39, 69 (PDF p. 20, 35)

questions.stem: ASA Standard I requires qualified anesthesia personnel to be present in the room during which anesthetics?
options: General anesthetics only, since regional patients can call for help
All general anesthetics, regional anesthetics, and monitored anesthesia care
Any anesthetic in which an airway device is placed
General and regional anesthetics, but not monitored anesthesia care
questions.explanation: Standard I: qualified anesthesia personnel shall be present throughout the conduct of all general anesthetics, regional anesthetics, and MAC. Instructor note: the most important monitor is the qualified anesthesia provider.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 9 (PDF p. 9)

questions.stem: Why is BP measured more often (every 1-5 minutes) during induction?
options: The ASA standard requires at least every minute during induction
Oscillometric readings are only accurate at intervals under 5 minutes
Short cuff intervals reduce the risk of cuff-related nerve injury
Anesthetic agents cause cardiac depression and vasodilation with unpredictable responses
questions.explanation: Higher frequency during induction reflects the cardiac depressant and vasodilating effects of anesthetics and unpredictable hemodynamic responses; frequency also rises in patients with limited reserve. The standard is at least every 5 minutes, not every minute, and frequent cycling INCREASES cuff complications like nerve injury.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 60 (PDF p. 61)

questions.stem: An edentulous patient is difficult to mask-ventilate. Why does adding an OPA help?
options: It lifts the tongue and improves the mask seal
It seals the glottis against gastric insufflation
It fills the space where the teeth were, preventing leaks at the lips
It displaces the soft palate to open the nasal passage
questions.explanation: The OPA's preformed, caudally facing concave shape follows the oropharyngeal anatomy and lifts the tongue. The lecture specifically notes it improves bag-mask seal in edentulous patients. It doesn't seal the glottis, and it isn't a nasal device.
questions.citation: Airway Equipment (McPherson): slide 5 (PDF p. 5)

questions.stem: The hospital's O2 manifold uses H-cylinders as its reserve. About how much O2 does each H-cylinder hold compared with an E-cylinder?
options: 1590 L vs about 660 L
6000-8000 L vs about 660 L
2000 L vs about 625 L
15,900 L vs about 1590 L
questions.explanation: From the cylinder table: O2 H-cylinders hold 6000-8000 L; E-cylinders hold about 625-700 L (660 L in the lecture's math). E-cylinders are the transport tank; H-cylinders are the hospital reservoir. 15,900 L and 1590 L are the N2O H- and E-cylinder values.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 7 (PDF p. 4)

questions.stem: Only a three-cable ECG system is available. Which configuration does the lecture list, and what is its drawback?
options: MCL5 plus aVF, with limited sensitivity
Lead II alone, with poor rhythm detection
V3 plus MCL5 plus aVF, with added artifact
V3 plus lead III, which requires a derived 12-lead
questions.explanation: Three-cable system: MCL5 plus aVF, with limitations in sensitivity. Five-cable options: V3 + MCL5 + aVF or V3 + lead III + aVF. Instructor note: 5-cable gets 6 views, 3-cable gets 2 views.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 57 (PDF p. 58)

questions.stem: For an oromaxillofacial procedure, the surgeon needs the tube connector directed away from the operative field and over the forehead. Which tube fits best?
options: Nasal RAE tube
Laser-resistant tube
Double-lumen tube
Armored (anode) tube
questions.explanation: RAE tubes (oral or nasal) have a preformed bend that routes the connector away from the surgical field and are used for oromaxillofacial and nasal procedures. Armored tubes are chosen for kink resistance, not connector position.
questions.citation: Airway Equipment (McPherson): slide 8 (PDF p. 8)

questions.stem: Which indicator dye color changes with absorbent exhaustion are correct? Select 3.
options: Ethyl violet: white to purple
Cresyl yellow: red to yellow
Ethyl violet: purple to white
Ethyl orange: orange to yellow
Ethyl orange: yellow to orange
Cresyl yellow: yellow to red
questions.explanation: As carbonate forms, pH falls and the dyes change: ethyl violet white to blue-violet, ethyl orange orange to yellow, cresyl yellow red to yellow. Ethyl violet is used most because the change is vivid and high contrast. Purple fading back toward white at rest is regeneration, not fresh absorbent.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 4 (PDF p. 2)

questions.stem: Which ECG setup steps does the lecture recommend before and during induction? Select 3.
options: Optimize waveform size
Use lead II alone for every patient
Print a baseline strip before induction
Place electrodes over the surgical prep site
Accept electrode placement by others without checking
Turn ST-segment monitoring on
questions.explanation: The lecture lists printing a baseline strip before induction, optimizing waveform size, and turning ST monitoring on, along with choosing leads for the patient. Surgical site and position may force lead changes, and you should trust but verify if others place electrodes.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 57 (PDF p. 58)

questions.stem: Why is invasive arterial pressure monitoring more hazardous in neonates than in adults?
options: Neonatal waveforms are overdamped, so readings are unreliable
Peripheral vessels lie closer to the great vessels, heart, and cerebral circulation
Flush volume is negligible compared with neonatal blood volume
Neonatal arteries are larger relative to body size, so emboli travel farther
questions.explanation: In pediatrics, smaller arteries, lower circulating volume, and peripheral vessels closer to the great vessels, heart, and cerebral circulation make placement harder and maintenance more hazardous. Flush devices infuse about 3-6 mL/hr, which DOES matter in neonates. Umbilical artery lines also carry a risk of aortic thrombosis and coarctation.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 71 (PDF p. 72)

questions.stem: Which is an active waste gas disposal route?
options: The nonrecirculating OR ventilation system
Wall suction or a dedicated evacuation system
A through-the-wall duct to the outside
A ceiling duct that vents passively to the roof
questions.explanation: Active disposal uses wall suction or a dedicated evacuation system (dedicated is preferred). Passive routes are the OR ventilation system (which must be nonrecirculating) or a through-the-wall conduit where gas flows through a duct in the wall, window, ceiling, or floor. Instructor note: passive systems are seen more in makeshift ORs.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 21 (PDF p. 11)

questions.stem: On this arterial waveform, which numbered point is read as the diastolic blood pressure?
options: Point 2
Point 4
Point 5
Point 6
questions.explanation: Point 6 is the end-diastolic pressure, the lowest point before the next upstroke, which is the DBP. Point 2 is systolic peak pressure, 4 is the dicrotic notch (aortic valve closure), and 5 is the diastolic runoff slope leading down to DBP.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 72 (PDF p. 73)

questions.stem: Which finding is a contraindication to placing a radial arterial line on that side?
options: Compromised collateral arterial supply to the hand
Planned one-lung ventilation
A weak radial pulse that needs ultrasound guidance
Need for continuous vasopressor titration
questions.explanation: Contraindications: compromised collateral supply, local infection, or proximal vascular injury or thrombosis that would prevent accurate readings. A weak pulse isn't a contraindication; ultrasound improves cannulation when pulses are weak or vessels small.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 67 (PDF p. 68)

questions.stem: O2 supply pressure falls during a case. Which numbered component responds by reducing, then stopping, N2O flow?
options: Component 1
Component 2
Component 3
Component 4
questions.explanation: Component 1 is the fail-safe valve. It sits in the N2O line but is controlled by O2 supply pressure, proportionally reducing and then stopping N2O as O2 pressure falls. Components 2 and 3 are the second-stage O2 and N2O pressure regulators, and 4 is the pressure relief valve.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slides 5, 34 (PDF p. 3, 17)

questions.stem: Which situations are indications for an invasive arterial line? Select 3.
options: Need for frequent blood gases and labs
Local infection at the planned cannulation site
Need for BP every 5 minutes in a stable patient
Compromised collateral flow to the hand
Planned one-lung ventilation for thoracic surgery
Vasoactive infusions requiring continuous titration
questions.explanation: Indications: expected rapid or extreme pressure changes, poor tolerance of instability, vasoactive drips needing titration, anticipated compromise of ventilation or oxygenation (cardiothoracic, major vascular, OLV), and frequent blood gases or labs. Every-5-minute BP is met by NIBP. Compromised collateral flow and local infection are contraindications.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 67 (PDF p. 68)

questions.stem: A fit 22-year-old athlete has a baseline HR in the low 50s, and the low-HR alarm keeps sounding. What does the lecture say about changing the alarm limit?
options: The limit should be raised so bradycardia is flagged sooner
The alarm may be silenced for the case once the baseline is documented
Alarm limits may never be changed from factory defaults
It may be adjusted, as long as the setting still meets practice standards
questions.explanation: If you change any alarm setting, you must make sure it still meets practice standards; the lecture uses this exact athlete example. Silencing or disabling alarms is a result of alarm fatigue that raises patient risk.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 20 (PDF p. 20)

questions.stem: Why are anesthesia face masks made of clear material?
options: To see lip color, exhaled condensation, secretions, vomit, and blood
To let you check cushion inflation and choose the mask size
To reduce dead space by showing how the mask sits on the face
To confirm exhaled CO2 by a color change in the plastic
questions.explanation: The clear mask lets you see lip color, condensation from exhalation, secretions, vomitus, and blood. Instructor note: pay attention to the quantity of fog, since condensation shows gas moving in and out. Transparency doesn't change dead space or measure CO2.
questions.citation: Airway Equipment (McPherson): slide 4 (PDF p. 4)

questions.stem: A cylinder storage room catches fire. Which cylinder safety device melts to let gas escape before the cylinder ruptures?
options: Yoke check valve
Fusible plug
Frangible disk
Spring-loaded pressure relief valve
questions.explanation: A fusible plug melts in a fire and vents gas. A frangible disk is a metal disk that breaks when pressure gets too high, and the spring-loaded relief valve opens above a pressure threshold; neither melts. The yoke check valve prevents backflow between cylinders; it isn't a cylinder relief device.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 17 (PDF p. 9)

questions.stem: ASA Standard 2.2 lists qualitative clinical signs that help evaluate ventilation. Which are they? Select 3.
options: Observation of the reservoir breathing bag
Auscultation of breath sounds
Palpation of a peripheral pulse
Skin and lip color
Pupil size
Chest excursion
questions.explanation: ASA 2.2 names chest excursion, observation of the reservoir bag, and auscultation of breath sounds as qualitative signs of ventilation, with continual expired CO2 monitoring on top. Skin color reflects oxygenation, a palpable pulse reflects circulation, and pupil size is a depth-of-anesthesia sign; all are qualitative but not ventilation signs.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 12 (PDF p. 12)

questions.stem: What is the approximate composition of wet soda lime?
options: Ca(OH)2 about 50%, water about 45%, NaOH and KOH about 5%
Ca(OH)2 about 80%, water about 15%, NaOH and KOH about 5%
NaOH about 80%, water about 15%, Ca(OH)2 about 5%
Ba(OH)2 about 80%, water about 15%, KOH about 5%
questions.explanation: Wet soda lime is roughly 80% calcium hydroxide, 15% water, and 5% sodium and potassium hydroxide. Calcium hydroxide is the bulk absorbent; NaOH and KOH act like catalysts. Barium hydroxide is Baralyme, a different absorbent.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 2 (PDF p. 1)

questions.stem: On machines that have one, where is the low-pressure check valve, and what does it prevent?
options: Near the common gas outlet, downstream of the vaporizers; backflow from the breathing circuit
Before the flowmeters; entry of N2O when O2 pressure is low
At the cylinder yoke; transfilling between cylinders
At the pipeline inlet; loss of gas when the pipeline is disconnected
questions.explanation: The low-pressure check valve sits near the common gas outlet, downstream of the flowmeters and vaporizers. It prevents backflow from the breathing circuit, helps ensure accurate delivery, and minimizes leaks (including the pumping effect). The other options describe the pipeline check valve, yoke check valve, and fail-safe.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 49 (PDF p. 25)

questions.stem: Which mechanism accounts for the largest share of heat loss in an anesthetized patient?
options: Evaporation
Convection
Radiation
Conduction
questions.explanation: Heat is lost through radiation, conduction, convection, and evaporation. Instructor note: radiation is the largest heat loss. Anesthesia also blocks afferent and efferent thermoregulation, so the patient can't compensate normally.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 80 (PDF p. 81)

questions.stem: Fresh gas flow through a Tec 6 is raised from 2 to 6 L/min with the dial unchanged. How is the dialed concentration maintained?
options: The dial restrictor automatically closes to reduce des vapor
Back pressure rises; the transducer opens the vapor valve to match, adding des
The sump heater raises temperature to increase vapor pressure
The bimetallic strip sends more gas through the sump
questions.explanation: The gas circuit restrictor creates back pressure proportional to fresh gas flow. The differential pressure transducer senses the gas and vapor circuits and moves a valve to equalize them, so vapor delivery rises with flow. The dial controls restrictor #2. There's no bimetallic strip in the Tec 6.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slides 62, 63 (PDF p. 31, 32)

questions.stem: Where is a traditional flowmeter indicator read?
options: At the bottom of the indicator
At the widest part of the indicator
At the top of the indicator
At the valve stop below the float
questions.explanation: The lecture's rule: the widest part of the indicator equals the amount of gas flow. That's where the annular space (the variable orifice) is defined.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 43 (PDF p. 22)

questions.stem: After the head is repositioned for surgery, the capnogram changes to this pattern. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: Cuff leak or tube withdrawn into the hypopharynx
Hypoventilation from a reduced ventilator rate
Rebreathing from an exhausted absorbent
Bronchospasm with a slow expiratory upstroke
questions.explanation: Slide 46 shows this pattern (normal breaths, then small irregular waves that don't reach a plateau) under decreasing ETCO2: ETT cuff leak, tube in the hypopharynx, or partial obstruction. Bronchospasm produces a shark fin, rebreathing raises the baseline, and hypoventilation raises ETCO2 with a normal shape.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 46 (PDF p. 47)

questions.stem: When an oropharyngeal airway is correctly seated, how is its concave surface oriented?
options: Facing cranially, pressing the soft palate upward
Facing laterally, displacing the tongue to one side
Facing the hard palate, holding the teeth apart
Facing caudally, following the oropharynx to lift the tongue
questions.explanation: The OPA has a caudally facing, concave surface whose preformed curve follows the oropharyngeal anatomy and lifts the tongue off the posterior pharynx.
questions.citation: Airway Equipment (McPherson): slide 5 (PDF p. 5)

questions.stem: In which events would the analyzer detect nitrogen in the expired gas? Select 3.
options: Air embolism
Hypoventilation
Endotracheal cuff leak
Anesthesia circuit leak
Vaporizer overdose
Malignant hyperthermia
questions.explanation: The analyzer table lists N2 (with CO2) for circuit leaks, cuff leaks, and poor mask or LMA fit, and CO2 plus N2 for air embolism. MH, hypoventilation, and airway obstruction are CO2 events; vaporizer overdose is an agent event.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 42 (PDF p. 42)

questions.stem: During laryngoscopy, the blade light is dim and flickering. Which setup step from the lecture would have prevented this problem?
options: Choosing a Miller blade instead of a Macintosh
Placing the patient in the sniffing position
Opening the video laryngoscope as the primary device
Checking spare batteries and having an extra blade and handle in reach
questions.explanation: Every direct laryngoscope has a handle, blade, and light source. The room setup (MS MAID) includes an additional blade and handle, and the instructor notes stress making sure spare batteries and battery equipment work. Positioning and blade choice don't fix a failing light.
questions.citation: Airway Equipment (McPherson): slide 11 (PDF p. 11); Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 3 (PDF p. 3)

questions.stem: An OR's recirculating ventilation system provides 18 air exchanges per hour, 2 of them fresh outside air. How does this compare with the requirement?
options: It meets requirements, because 15-21 total exchanges are provided
It falls short, because at least 3 exchanges must be fresh outside air
It exceeds requirements, because only 1 fresh exchange is needed
It meets requirements, because recirculated air is filtered of anesthetic gas
questions.explanation: ORs need 15-21 air exchanges per hour, and at least 3 must be fresh outside air. Filtering doesn't remove anesthetic gases, which is why recirculating systems can carry contamination between ORs.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 17 (PDF p. 9)

questions.stem: Why does AANA Standard 9 recommend variable-pitch pulse oximetry alarms?
options: They replace the need to set upper and lower alarm limits
They reduce how often false alarms sound during the case
They measure oxygen saturation more accurately than tones
They let you hear subtle SpO2 changes without looking at the monitor
questions.explanation: Variable-pitch tones allow early recognition of subtle oxygenation changes through hearing. Alarm limits and audible warnings must still be used; pitch doesn't change measurement accuracy or false-alarm frequency.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 18 (PDF p. 18)

questions.stem: Shortly after intubation, the ventilator displays this pressure-volume loop. Which problem best explains its shape?
options: Increased airway resistance during expiration, as in bronchospasm
Abnormally increased compliance, as in emphysema
A leak in the breathing circuit
Increased airway resistance during inspiration, as in a bitten ETT
questions.explanation: The loop is closed but widened, with the expiratory limb bowed out, the lecture's pattern for increased resistance on expiration (bronchospasm). A kinked or bitten ETT bows the inspiratory limb. A leak leaves the loop open, and increased compliance makes it tall and steep toward the volume axis.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 29 (PDF p. 29)

questions.stem: To estimate how much N2O remains in an E-cylinder, which pieces of information do you need? Select 2.
options: Current total cylinder weight
The rated filling pressure
The retest date marking
Tare weight stamped on the cylinder
The cylinder serial number
The current gauge pressure
questions.explanation: N2O pressure stays at 745 psig while liquid remains, so the gauge can't tell you contents; the instructor noted you have to weigh the cylinder. Subtracting the stamped tare weight from the current weight gives the mass of N2O left. Filling pressure, serial number, and retest markings don't change with use.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slides 9, 14 (PDF p. 5, 7)

questions.stem: Which complications of invasive arterial monitoring are listed in the lecture? Select 3.
options: Nerve injury
Thrombosis
Air embolism from pressurized flushing
Methemoglobinemia
Compartment syndrome from repeated cuff inflation
Pneumothorax
questions.explanation: Complications listed: hematoma, thrombosis, ischemia, embolism, infection, nerve injury, hemorrhage, and air embolism from pressurized flushing. Compartment syndrome is listed as a NIBP complication; pneumothorax and methemoglobinemia aren't arterial line complications in the lecture.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 69 (PDF p. 70)

questions.stem: In a 3-kg neonate on sidestream capnography, which factors can make ETCO2 read falsely low? Select 3.
options: Hyperthermia
Bicarbonate administration
Leak around a cuffless tube
Use of an adult breathing circuit
Rebreathing from an exhausted absorbent
Sidestream aspiration of up to about 200 mL/min
questions.explanation: Slide 49: sidestream systems may aspirate about 200 mL/min, a large fraction of ventilation in small infants; cuffless tubes can produce falsely low ETCO2; and an adult circuit used for pediatrics adds dead space. Hyperthermia and bicarbonate raise CO2 load, and rebreathing raises the baseline.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 49 (PDF p. 50)

questions.stem: Hospital vacuum to a closed-reservoir scavenging interface fails during a case. Which findings are expected? Select 2.
options: Excess suction pulls gas out through the APL valve
The positive-pressure (pop-off) relief valve vents waste gas into the room
Negative pressure is transmitted to the breathing circuit
The negative-pressure (pop-in) relief valve opens to room air
The interface reservoir bag collapses
The interface reservoir bag distends
questions.explanation: With vacuum failure or insufficient suction, waste gas accumulates, so the reservoir bag distends and pressure builds until the pop-off valve opens and vents gas into the room. Bag collapse, pop-in opening, and negative pressure on the circuit are the findings with EXCESSIVE suction.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 20 (PDF p. 10)

questions.stem: Which LMA Supreme feature protects the airway tube from occlusion if the patient bites down?
options: Modified cuff shape
Integrated bite block
Fixation tab
Drain tube opening
questions.explanation: The labeled LMA Supreme diagram shows an integrated bite block along the airway tube. The drain tube allows gastric drainage, the fixation tab secures the device, and the modified cuff forms the seal.
questions.citation: Airway Equipment (McPherson): slide 14 (PDF p. 14)

questions.stem: During bag-mask ventilation, the chest rises slightly, but there's no ETCO2 waveform and SpO2 is falling. How should ventilation be judged?
options: Inadequate, since objective measures show no gas exchange
Adequate, since chest movement is present
Adequate, until SpO2 falls below 90%
Indeterminate until exhaled tidal volume is checked
questions.explanation: Mask ventilation is judged by clinical signs (chest movement, gas leak) AND objective measures (sustained SpO2, waveform ETCO2, peak airway pressure, exhaled volume). Slight chest movement with no ETCO2 and falling SpO2 means ventilation is failing now. Waiting for 90% or an extra measurement delays correction.
questions.citation: Airway Equipment (McPherson): slide 4 (PDF p. 4)

questions.stem: Which events can deliver a hypoxic mixture despite a working fail-safe valve and proportioning system? Select 3.
options: Nitrogen contamination of the O2 pipeline
O2 supply pressure falling to 20 psig with N2O on
Hanging an N2O cylinder on the O2 yoke
N2O set at 4 L/min with O2 turned to 0.5 L/min
Crossed O2 and N2O pipelines
A cracked O2 flowmeter tube
questions.explanation: Both safety systems sense only pressure, not O2 itself, so crossed pipelines and nitrogen contamination slip past them (the lecture cites real events from 2024 and 2019). A cracked flowmeter tube leaks O2 downstream of both. Low O2 supply pressure triggers the fail-safe, a low O2 to N2O ratio triggers the proportioner, and PISS prevents an N2O cylinder from fitting the O2 yoke.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slides 46, 48 (PDF p. 23, 24)

questions.stem: You're working at another hospital with a different brand of wall outlets. Which connection is MOST likely not to fit your usual hoses?
options: The quick connector at the wall outlet
The common gas outlet fitting
The PISS yoke on the O2 cylinder
The DISS fitting at the machine inlet
questions.explanation: Quick connectors are gas specific per manufacturer, with no standardization. DISS threads are nationally standardized, PISS is standardized for cylinders, and common gas outlet connections are standardized sizes.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slides 29, 30 (PDF p. 15)

questions.stem: On this arterial waveform, which numbered point is read as the diastolic blood pressure?
options: Point 2
Point 4
Point 5
Point 6
questions.explanation: Point 6 is the end-diastolic pressure, the lowest point before the next upstroke, which is the DBP. Point 2 is systolic peak pressure, 4 is the dicrotic notch (aortic valve closure), and 5 is the diastolic runoff slope leading down to DBP.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 72 (PDF p. 73)

questions.stem: A variable bypass vaporizer tops out at 5%. Which agent could NOT be delivered at 1 MAC (age 40) with it?
options: Isoflurane
Halothane
Sevoflurane
Desflurane
questions.explanation: MAC values: des 6.6%, sevo 1.8%, iso 1.17%, halothane 0.76%. Only des exceeds 5%, which is one reason it needs its own vaporizer calibrated to 12% or higher. Sevo vaporizers go to 8%.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slides 50, 58 (PDF p. 25, 29)

questions.stem: During a low-flow anesthetic (O2 0.5 L/min plus air), the inspired O2 concentration slowly falls over an hour with no change in settings. What explains this?
options: The proportioning system reduces O2 flow at low total flows
Rebreathed CO2 displaces O2 from the analyzer membrane
Metabolic O2 consumption lowers circuit O2 when little fresh gas is added
The galvanic sensor drifts upward as it is consumed
questions.explanation: Slide 37: monitoring is especially important during low-flow anesthesia because metabolic O2 use can lower circuit FiO2. With little fresh gas replacing what the patient consumes, inspired O2 drifts down. The proportioning system links O2 to N2O, not to air.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 37 (PDF p. 37)

questions.stem: How should an arterial pressure transducer be zeroed?
options: Opened to atmosphere at the level of the catheter insertion site
Zeroed with the stopcock closed to air at the level of the floor
Opened to atmosphere at the level of the right atrium
Zeroed against the NIBP reading at any height
questions.explanation: Slide 66: zero and level the transducer to the appropriate reference point, usually the right atrium. Zeroing sets atmospheric pressure as the reference; leveling to the RA removes the hydrostatic error from gravity. The insertion site isn't the reference, and matching to a cuff isn't zeroing.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 66 (PDF p. 67)

questions.stem: Absorbent may have dried out over a long weekend, and only sevoflurane and desflurane are available. Which statement is correct?
options: Sevo is safe with dry absorbent because it forms neither CO nor compound A
Sevo avoids CO, but dry absorbent promotes compound A; replace the absorbent
Either agent is safe if FGF is raised to wash out byproducts
Des is preferred because it forms compound A only with moist absorbent
questions.explanation: Sevo lacks the -O-CHF2 group, so it doesn't form CO, but warm, dry absorbent promotes compound A. Des produces the most CO with desiccated absorbent. The recommendation is not to use absorbent known or suspected to be desiccated with either.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slides 6, 7 (PDF p. 3, 4)

questions.stem: After a vasodilator infusion is started, radial arterial pressure reads lower than a simultaneous central aortic pressure. What explains this?
options: Peripheral wave reflection always makes radial higher, so the reading is an error
Vasodilators overdamp the transducer
The radial transducer is leveled above the heart
Changes in hand vascular resistance make radial underestimate central pressure
questions.explanation: Radial SBP usually EXCEEDS aortic SBP from wave reflection, but the lecture notes radial pressures can underestimate central pressures when hand vascular resistance changes, and vasodilating drugs can accentuate the discrepancy. A mis-leveled transducer would shift all readings, not specifically after a vasodilator.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 70 (PDF p. 71)

questions.stem: Under the ASA standard, which situations require continuous exhaled CO2 monitoring in addition to clinical signs? Select 2.
options: Local infiltration with no sedation
An interscalene block with minimal anxiolysis
Deep sedation
A spinal anesthetic with the patient fully awake
Regional anesthesia with minimal sedation
Moderate sedation
questions.explanation: Moderate or deep sedation: continual observation of clinical signs AND continuous exhaled CO2. Local or regional anesthesia with minimal or no sedation: continual observation of qualitative clinical signs is enough.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slides 47, 94 (PDF p. 48, 95)
