questions.explanation: Every patient receiving anesthesia shall have the ECG continuously displayed from the beginning of anesthesia until preparing to leave the anesthetizing location.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 13 (PDF p. 13)

questions.stem: The low-pressure leak check fails, and the leak is traced to the CO2 absorber housing. Which problems could be responsible? Select 3.
options: A cracked flowmeter tube
Absorbent granules on the gasket
A defective N2O pipeline quick connect
A worn O2 cylinder yoke washer
An open drain petcock
Loose screws on the absorber housing
questions.explanation: Low-pressure leaks occur most commonly at the CO2 absorber: loose screws, worn gaskets, granules on the gaskets, and an open petcock. Quick connects and yoke washers are high-pressure leaks, and a cracked flowmeter tube is a low-pressure leak but not at the absorber.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 13 (PDF p. 7)

questions.stem: An N2O E-cylinder is left in a room at 40 C. What state is its contents in?
options: All liquid, because heat raises cylinder pressure
Mostly solid, because rapid evaporation cools the liquid
Liquid and gas at 745 psig, as at room temperature
All gas, because 40 C is above N2O's critical temperature
questions.explanation: N2O's critical temperature is about 36 C. Above it, no amount of pressure keeps N2O liquid, so the cylinder contains only gas at a pressure above 745 psig. Below it, liquid and gas coexist and the gauge holds at 745 psig at 20 C.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 14 (PDF p. 7)

questions.stem: An internationally sourced cylinder painted white and black has valve holes at positions 1 and 5. Which yoke should it hang on?
options: Nitrogen
Oxygen
Nitrous oxide
Medical air
questions.explanation: International coding: air is white and black, O2 is solid white. PISS for air is 1 and 5; O2 is 2 and 5 and N2O is 3 and 5. Both the color and the pins point to medical air.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slides 7, 18 (PDF p. 4, 9)

questions.stem: During the machine check, the galvanic O2 sensor exposed to room air reads 30%. What is the appropriate step?
options: Accept it, since a high O2 reading errs on the side of safety
Calibrate the sensor against 100% O2 only and proceed
Move the sensor to the expiratory limb and recheck it
Recalibrate to 21% room air and recheck; replace the sensor if it fails
questions.explanation: Removable galvanic sensors are commonly calibrated against room air (21%) daily, after prolonged use, and some also need occasional 100% calibration. A falsely high reading could hide a hypoxic mixture, so it isn't 'safe.' The sensor belongs in the inspired limb.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 36 (PDF p. 36)

questions.stem: Which are RESULTS of alarm fatigue, as opposed to its causes? Select 3.
options: Delayed or missed recognition of critical events
Ignoring or disabling alarms
Difficulty localizing alarms in a noisy OR
Increased patient safety risk
High numbers of false or noncritical alarms
Alarms interfering with team communication
questions.explanation: Results: ignoring or disabling alarms, delayed or missed recognition of critical events, and increased risk to patients. The last three are contributing factors: many false alarms, difficulty localizing alarms in noise, and interference with communication.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 19 (PDF p. 19)

questions.stem: Mid-case, the O2 pipeline hose is pulled from the wall and the O2 supply low-pressure alarm sounds. The backup O2 cylinder is closed. What is the FIRST action?
options: Open the backup O2 cylinder on the machine
Switch the patient to the auxiliary O2 flowmeter
Increase N2O flow to maintain total fresh gas flow
Press the O2 flush to keep the bag full
questions.explanation: The machine uses the cylinder (regulated to about 45 psi) whenever pipeline pressure is lower, but only if the cylinder is open. The flush and the auxiliary flowmeter draw from the same O2 supply that just failed, and the fail-safe will reduce and then stop N2O as O2 pressure falls.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slides 26, 33, 44 (PDF p. 13, 17, 22)

questions.stem: Which blade descriptions match the lecture? Select 2.
options: Miller: lifts the epiglottis by stretching the glossoepiglottic ligament
Macintosh: sharply curved with a large flange, lifts the epiglottis indirectly
Miller: sharply curved with a large flange, tip in the vallecula
Miller: long and straight, curve begins about 2 inches from the tip, lifts the epiglottis directly
Macintosh: curve begins about 2 inches from the tip
Macintosh: long and straight, traps the epiglottis
questions.explanation: The Miller is a long, straight blade with the curve starting about 2 inches from the tip, used by epiglottic entrapment (direct lift). The Macintosh is sharply curved with a large flange, lifting the epiglottis indirectly by stretching the glossoepiglottic ligament.
questions.citation: Airway Equipment (McPherson): slide 11 (PDF p. 11)

questions.stem: A fast-flush test shows a slow return to baseline with no oscillations, and the waveform looks rounded. What should you expect, and what should you check?
options: Overdamping underestimating SBP; check for bubbles, clot, or kinks
Underdamping underestimating SBP; add extension tubing
Overdamping overestimating SBP; lower the transducer
Underdamping overestimating SBP; check for bubbles, clot, or kinks
questions.explanation: The fast-flush test gauges damping from the resonant waves after the flush. No oscillations and a slow return mean an overdamped system, which underestimates SBP. Air bubbles, clot, kinks, excess tubing, and stopcocks degrade fidelity; extension tubing makes it worse.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slides 65, 69 (PDF p. 66, 70)

questions.stem: Which medical gas cylinders contain both liquid and gas at room temperature? Select 2.
options: Helium
Carbon dioxide
Nitrous oxide
Medical air
Oxygen
Nitrogen
questions.explanation: From the lecture's cylinder table, N2O (745 psi) and CO2 (838 psi) are liquid/gas; O2, air, and helium are gases. For liquid/gas cylinders, pressure stays constant while liquid remains, so contents are found by weight.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 7 (PDF p. 4)

questions.stem: ETCO2 has risen from 36 to 44 mmHg with unchanged ventilator settings, and the inspired CO2 baseline is still zero. Which cause is ruled out?
options: Rebreathing
Increased CO2 production
Absorption of insufflated CO2
Decreased elimination from hypoventilation
questions.explanation: Rebreathing (exhausted absorbent, bad valves, low FGF) shows up as a baseline that doesn't return to zero. A zero baseline rules it out and leaves increased production, increased delivery (laparoscopy), or decreased elimination.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slides 43, 50 (PDF p. 43, 51)

questions.stem: After failed intubation and failed supraglottic airway rescue, the patient can't be oxygenated and SpO2 is falling rapidly. What is the next step?
options: Cricothyrotomy through the cricothyroid membrane
Fiberoptic intubation through the failed SGA
Another direct laryngoscopy attempt with a Miller blade
Continued two-person mask ventilation with an OPA
questions.explanation: Cricothyrotomy is a lifesaving emergency procedure and the final option for 'cannot intubate, cannot ventilate' in every airway algorithm. Once oxygenation has failed by all routes, further attempts at the same techniques delay oxygenation. Approaches: needle, percutaneous, or surgical.
questions.citation: Airway Equipment (McPherson): slide 15 (PDF p. 15)

questions.stem: Which statements about laser-resistant endotracheal tubes are correct? Select 2.
options: Laser tubes remove the need to adjust O2 or N2O concentration
N2O is safer than O2 because it doesn't support combustion
The cuff is laser resistant, so air is the preferred fill
Conventional PVC tubes are flammable, so noncombustible tubes are used
The cuff isn't laser resistant, so it's filled with saline or water and dye
Airway fire is a minor risk once a laser tube is used
questions.explanation: Airway fire from ETT ignition is the most serious laser danger. PVC tubes are flammable, so noncombustible tubes are used, but their cuffs aren't laser resistant and are filled with saline or water and dye. O2 and N2O concentration still matter, since both support ignition.
questions.citation: Airway Equipment (McPherson): slide 9 (PDF p. 9)

questions.stem: After refilling a variable bypass vaporizer, the liquid is visibly above the maximum mark in the sight glass. What should happen before it is used?
options: Drain it to the specified level
Use it normally, since overfilling only extends run time
Tilt it briefly to redistribute the excess liquid
Run it at a low dial setting until the level falls
questions.explanation: Overfilling risks liquid contaminating the bypass chamber or outlet and overdosing the patient. The lecture's intervention: turn the vaporizer off, keep it in the correct position, and fill only to the specified level. Tilting is exactly what sends liquid into the bypass.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 70 (PDF p. 35)

questions.stem: Which conditions can impair pulse oximeter readings? Select 3.
options: Nail polish
Electrocautery
Supplemental O2 by nasal cannula
Ambient light
A PaO2 above 300 mmHg
A regular heart rate of 55 with good perfusion
questions.explanation: The lecture lists motion, low perfusion, hypothermia, dyes, nail polish, ambient light, electrocautery, and infrared systems. High PaO2, supplemental O2, and a slow regular rhythm with good perfusion don't impair readings, though supplemental O2 does delay detection of hypoventilation.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 78 (PDF p. 79)

questions.stem: The fast-flush test estimates which two dynamic properties of an arterial pressure system?
options: Mean arterial pressure and pulse pressure of the waveform
Zero offset of the transducer and its height above the heart
Systolic overshoot and diastolic undershoot values only
Damping (amplitude ratio) and natural frequency (oscillation interval)
questions.explanation: The fast-flush test estimates damping from the amplitude ratio of the resonant waves and natural frequency from the oscillation interval. High-fidelity monitoring needs a dynamic response appropriate for the arterial waveform's broad frequency content.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 65 (PDF p. 66)

questions.stem: An O2 E-cylinder with a 5 L internal volume reads 500 psig. Using Boyle's law at 14.7 psi atmospheric pressure, about how much O2 is available?
options: About 34 L
About 170 L
About 330 L
About 660 L
questions.explanation: P1V1 = P2V2: 500 psi x 5 L = 14.7 psi x V2, so V2 is about 170 L. The lecture's full-cylinder version (1900 x 5 / 14.7) gives about 660 L, so 500 psig is roughly a quarter.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slides 12, 13 (PDF p. 6, 7)

questions.stem: Fresh gas flow through a Tec 6 is raised from 2 to 6 L/min with the dial unchanged. How is the dialed concentration maintained?
options: The dial restrictor automatically closes to reduce des vapor
The bimetallic strip sends more gas through the sump
The sump heater raises temperature to increase vapor pressure
Back pressure rises; the transducer opens the vapor valve to match, adding des
questions.explanation: The gas circuit restrictor creates back pressure proportional to fresh gas flow. The differential pressure transducer senses the gas and vapor circuits and moves a valve to equalize them, so vapor delivery rises with flow. The dial controls restrictor #2. There's no bimetallic strip in the Tec 6.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slides 62, 63 (PDF p. 31, 32)

questions.stem: Why is ethyl violet the most commonly used indicator dye?
options: Its color change is vivid and high contrast at a pH between NaOH and CaCO3
It never regenerates after the absorbent is exhausted
It changes color only when compound A begins to form
It can't be bleached by intense OR lighting
questions.explanation: Ethyl violet is chosen because its white-to-purple change is vivid and high contrast at a pH intermediate between NaOH and CaCO3. It can still regenerate at rest and be bleached by intense light, which is why color isn't relied on.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 4 (PDF p. 2)

questions.stem: Which complications are listed for NIBP (not invasive arterial) monitoring? Select 3.
options: Compartment syndrome
Air embolism from pressurized flushing
Catheter-related infection
Nerve injury
Arterial thrombosis
Interference with an IV infusion
questions.explanation: NIBP complications: nerve injury, compartment syndrome, and interference with IV infusions (so use the contralateral limb). Air embolism from flushing, thrombosis, and infection are arterial line complications.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slides 62, 69 (PDF p. 63, 70)

questions.stem: Why does general anesthesia make patients vulnerable to hypothermia?
options: It raises basal metabolic heat production
It inhibits afferent and efferent thermoregulatory control
It stops radiant heat loss from the skin
It resets the thermoregulatory threshold upward
questions.explanation: Heat production reflects metabolism balanced against environmental heat transfer. General and regional anesthesia inhibit afferent and efferent thermoregulatory control, and anesthetics alter basal metabolism, muscular activity, sympathetic responses, vascular tone, and hormonal responses. Radiation remains the largest heat loss.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 80 (PDF p. 81)

questions.stem: Why does the lecture single out careful FiO2 management during pediatric airway surgery?
options: Galvanic sensors are inaccurate in children
Pediatric circuits can't measure FiO2
Fire risk
Retinopathy risk from any O2 above 21%
questions.explanation: Slide 38 notes that careful FiO2 management is especially important in pediatric airway surgery because of fire risk. Oxidizer concentration is one of the three ignition factors for airway fire.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 38 (PDF p. 38)

questions.stem: A lightly sedated patient with several loose front teeth develops tongue-based obstruction. Which airway adjunct is the better choice?
options: Oropharyngeal airway, since it best lifts the tongue
Bite block alone to keep the mouth open
Nasopharyngeal airway, avoiding dental contact and gagging
Larger oropharyngeal airway to spread pressure across the teeth
questions.explanation: OPA complications include dental damage and stimulation of airway reflexes, and awake or lightly sedated patients tolerate NPAs better. An NPA avoids the teeth; its most common complication is epistaxis.
questions.citation: Airway Equipment (McPherson): slides 5, 6 (PDF p. 5, 6)

questions.stem: A sedated patient's capnogram is shown (dotted line = 45 mmHg). The respiratory rate is 6. What does this pattern indicate?
options: Hyperventilation
Bronchospasm
Rebreathing from an exhausted absorbent
Hypoventilation
questions.explanation: Normal-shaped waveforms with a plateau above 45 mmHg and long intervals between breaths is the lecture's hypoventilation pattern. Hyperventilation shows frequent, low waves; rebreathing raises the BASELINE; bronchospasm gives a shark fin.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 46 (PDF p. 47)

questions.stem: Palpating down the midline from the thyroid notch, where is the cricothyroid membrane found?
options: Between the hyoid bone and the superior thyroid cartilage
Below the cricoid cartilage at the first tracheal ring
Between the inferior thyroid cartilage and the superior cricoid cartilage
At the level of the thyroid notch itself
questions.explanation: The CTM is a fibroelastic membrane over the tracheal mucosa, attached to the inferior border of the thyroid cartilage and the superior edge of the cricoid cartilage. Moving down from the thyroid prominence, it's the space just above the cricoid.
questions.citation: Airway Equipment (McPherson): slide 15 (PDF p. 15)

questions.stem: A long sevoflurane anesthetic runs at 0.5 L/min fresh gas flow, and the absorbent canister is warm. Which change most directly reduces compound A production?
options: Increase fresh gas flow
Switch to barium hydroxide lime
Increase the sevoflurane concentration
Let the absorbent dry out
questions.explanation: Compound A is promoted by warmer, drier absorbent, higher agent concentration, and LOWER fresh gas flow. Raising FGF works against it. Drying the absorbent and raising agent concentration both increase compound A.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 6 (PDF p. 3)

questions.stem: After extubation, the circuit is disconnected and the provider squeezes the reservoir bag to empty it before the next case. What is the problem?
options: It creates negative pressure at the scavenger
It damages the unidirectional valves
It desiccates the CO2 absorbent
It spills anesthetic gas directly into the room
questions.explanation: The lecture lists emptying the breathing circuit while it is disconnected from the patient as a technique error that spills anesthetic gases directly into room air. Desiccation comes from prolonged high gas flows, not from squeezing the bag.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 14 (PDF p. 7)

questions.stem: A patient in cardiac arrest is intubated. Breath sounds are bilateral and the chest rises, but ETCO2 is very low with small waveforms. What is the best interpretation?
options: Hyperventilation is lowering ETCO2; reduce the rate
The tube is likely tracheal; low ETCO2 reflects low pulmonary blood flow
Low ETCO2 proves esophageal placement; reintubate immediately
The sampling line is kinked; replace it before continuing
questions.explanation: Box 18.1 lists low cardiac output or arrest under decreased CO2 delivery. With bilateral breath sounds, chest rise, and persistent (if small) waveforms, placement is supported; the low value reflects limited pulmonary flow. That's why compression quality is judged by trying to keep ETCO2 at least 10 mmHg.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slides 43, 93 (PDF p. 43, 94)

questions.stem: As agent vaporizes and the Aladin cassette cools, how is delivered concentration held steady?
options: The CPU monitors agent temperature and adjusts flow through the flow control valve
A heater brings the cassette back to 39 C
The cassette automatically increases total fresh gas flow
A bimetallic strip inside the cassette opens the chamber wider
questions.explanation: The CPU monitors agent temperature in every cassette and adjusts how much agent-laden gas the flow control valve adds to the bypass gas. Metal plates and fans under the cassette help stabilize temperature. Bimetallic strips are variable bypass features; heating to 39 C is the Tec 6.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 67 (PDF p. 34)

questions.stem: A variable bypass vaporizer's dial won't turn off zero. What is the MOST likely reason?
options: The dial turns clockwise to increase concentration
The release button must be pressed before turning counterclockwise
The vaporizer is overfilled, locking the dial
The vaporizer is in transport (T) mode on the manifold
questions.explanation: The interlock safety mechanism requires pushing a button and rotating counterclockwise from the locked (closed) position to open. T mode is for securing the vaporizer during transport, and overfilling doesn't lock the dial.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 59 (PDF p. 30)

questions.stem: Which pressure-to-compliance pairings are correct? Select 2.
options: Peak inspiratory pressure reflects dynamic compliance
Peak inspiratory pressure reflects static compliance
Plateau pressure reflects dynamic compliance
Plateau pressure reflects airway resistance alone
Peak inspiratory pressure reflects chest wall compliance alone
Plateau pressure reflects static compliance
questions.explanation: PIP is the highest pressure during inspiration and reflects dynamic compliance (resistance plus compliance). Plateau is measured during an inspiratory pause with no flow and mirrors static compliance. Instructor note: know the definitions.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 26 (PDF p. 26)

questions.stem: During procedural sedation, the capnogram shows this sequence. What is the best interpretation?
options: A cuff leak in an endotracheal tube
Periods of shallow breathing and apnea from sedation
Cardiac oscillations during the expiratory pause
Bronchospasm with incomplete exhalation
questions.explanation: Slide 46 shows this pattern under decreased ETCO2 from apnea or sedation: small, irregular waves and a flat stretch, followed by one large breath carrying accumulated CO2. It's a sedation-depth warning. Pulse oximetry would lag behind, since it's a poor indicator of ventilation.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 46 (PDF p. 47)

questions.stem: With a copper kettle, the O2 flow through the kettle is increased while the main flowmeter flow is unchanged. What happens to the delivered concentration?
options: It stays the same, because copper holds temperature constant
It increases, because more saturated vapor joins the same main flow
It decreases, because more O2 dilutes the vapor
It stays the same, because the kettle is concentration-calibrated
questions.explanation: The kettle's dedicated O2 flow bubbles through liquid agent and leaves carrying saturated vapor, which then joins fresh gas from the main flowmeters. More kettle flow means more vapor into an unchanged main flow, so concentration rises. The kettle isn't concentration-calibrated, which is why calculations are required.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 74 (PDF p. 37)

questions.stem: A patient has known left subclavian artery stenosis. Why is a left radial arterial line a poor choice?
options: Radial lines are contraindicated in all vascular patients
Proximal vascular disease on that side prevents accurate readings
Left-sided lines can't be zeroed to the right atrium
The left radial has no collateral flow
questions.explanation: Contraindications include compromised collateral supply, local infection, and proximal vascular injury or thrombosis that would prevent accurate readings. A proximal stenosis makes pressure distal to it read falsely low.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 67 (PDF p. 68)

questions.stem: Which cricothyrotomy approaches does the lecture list? Select 3.
options: Percutaneous cricothyrotomy
Needle cricothyrotomy
Surgical cricothyrotomy
Formal tracheostomy through the tracheal rings
Blind nasal intubation
Retrograde wire intubation
questions.explanation: The lecture lists three approaches to the cricothyroid membrane: needle, percutaneous, and surgical. Tracheostomy enters through tracheal rings, and retrograde and blind nasal techniques are intubation methods, not front-of-neck access.
questions.citation: Airway Equipment (McPherson): slide 15 (PDF p. 15)

questions.stem: How is a hybrid flowmeter described in the lecture?
options: Electronic control with a glass flow tube
A glass tube with a fluted O2 knob only
A digital mixer with no manual backup
Needle-valve control with an electronic flow display
questions.explanation: The lecture lists three flowmeter types: mechanical (glass tubes with needle valves), electronic gas mixers (digital interface to control flow), and hybrid (needle valve control with an electronic display).
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 40 (PDF p. 20)

questions.stem: Hospital vacuum to a closed-reservoir scavenging interface fails during a case. Which findings are expected? Select 2.
options: The interface reservoir bag distends
The negative-pressure (pop-in) relief valve opens to room air
Excess suction pulls gas out through the APL valve
The interface reservoir bag collapses
The positive-pressure (pop-off) relief valve vents waste gas into the room
Negative pressure is transmitted to the breathing circuit
questions.explanation: With vacuum failure or insufficient suction, waste gas accumulates, so the reservoir bag distends and pressure builds until the pop-off valve opens and vents gas into the room. Bag collapse, pop-in opening, and negative pressure on the circuit are the findings with EXCESSIVE suction.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 20 (PDF p. 10)

questions.stem: Besides the disconnect alarms, which other ventilator alarms does the lecture list? Select 3.
options: Low peak inspiratory pressure
Low exhaled tidal volume
High PEEP
Low exhaled CO2
High peak inspiratory pressure
Negative pressure
questions.explanation: Disconnect alarms: low PIP, low exhaled tidal volume, low exhaled CO2. Other alarms listed: high PIP, high PEEP, sustained high airway pressure, negative pressure, and low O2 supply pressure.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 33 (PDF p. 33)

questions.stem: During CPR, the intubated patient's capnogram changes as shown. What is the MOST likely explanation?
options: Hyperventilation from overly rapid bagging
Sampling line disconnection
Esophageal migration of the tube
Return of spontaneous circulation
questions.explanation: Low, flat CO2 waves during CPR reflect low pulmonary blood flow. A sudden rise in ETCO2 is the lecture's sign of ROSC, as CO2-rich blood reaches the lungs again. Hyperventilation lowers ETCO2, and esophageal placement or a disconnection would make CO2 fade or vanish, not jump.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 46 (PDF p. 47)

questions.stem: A CO2 E-cylinder (stored as liquid and gas) reads 838 psi. What does this tell you about its contents?
options: It is full, holding about 1590 L
It is about half full
Liquid remains, but the gauge can't show how much
It holds only gas, with volume proportional to pressure
questions.explanation: Like N2O, CO2 is stored as liquid and gas, so the gauge reads the vapor pressure (838 psi at room temperature) as long as liquid remains. Contents can't be judged from pressure; the cylinder must be weighed. Pressure falls in proportion to volume only after the liquid is gone.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slides 7, 14 (PDF p. 4, 7)

questions.stem: During an MH crisis with rising CO2, acidosis, and temperature, a PaO2 of 70 mmHg shows a lower SpO2 than you'd expect at baseline. Why?
options: The curve shifts right, lowering hemoglobin's O2 affinity
Hyperthermia makes pulse oximetry read falsely low
High CO2 blocks the 940 nm infrared signal
The curve shifts left, raising hemoglobin's O2 affinity
questions.explanation: Hypercapnia, acidosis, and hyperthermia all shift the curve right, lowering Hb's O2 affinity. At the same PaO2, saturation is lower, though O2 unloading to tissues improves.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slides 43, 74 (PDF p. 43, 75)

questions.stem: According to the lecture's variable bypass vaporizer features, how does the vaporizer handle elevation changes?
options: It compensates for elevation changes
It underdoses at altitude and must be turned up
It overdoses at altitude and must be recalibrated
It can't be used above sea level
questions.explanation: The lecture's 'fun facts' on slide 52 state that the variable bypass vaporizer compensates for elevation changes, along with the 200 mL vapor per mL liquid and vol% x FGF x 3 rules.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 52 (PDF p. 26)

questions.stem: A large pleural effusion is drained during surgery. Under unchanged volume-control settings, PIP and plateau pressure both fall. What does this show?
options: Decreased airway resistance after the drainage
Decreased compliance from lung re-expansion
A new breathing circuit leak lowering pressures
Increased compliance from resolution of a restrictive factor
questions.explanation: Pleural effusion is on the lecture's list of causes of decreased compliance (PIP and plateau both up). Removing it reverses that: less pressure for the same volume, which is increased compliance. A resistance change would move PIP without moving plateau.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slides 28, 32 (PDF p. 28, 32)

questions.stem: Which surgical-field item does the lecture flag specifically for fire prevention?
options: Lap sponges
Lighted instruments
Surgical drapes secured in place
Suction machine level
questions.explanation: The surgical field checklist on slide 56: case status and critical points, blood loss (laps, sponges, suction level, floor), drapes in place, surgeon communication, and lighted instruments for fire prevention.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 56 (PDF p. 57)

questions.stem: In a closed-circuit anesthetic, all of a patient's CO2 production (200 mL/min) is absorbed by a 1,000 g soda lime canister. About how long until the canister is exhausted?
options: About 2 hours
About 8 hours
About 22 hours
About 43 hours
questions.explanation: 100 g of soda lime absorbs about 26 L of CO2, so 1,000 g holds about 260 L. At 0.2 L/min, 260 / 0.2 = 1,300 minutes, about 22 hours. In practice, channeling and higher FGF change how much exhaled gas actually reaches the absorbent.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 2 (PDF p. 1)

questions.stem: Both arms are tucked and unavailable for a noninvasive cuff. Which alternative site does the lecture list?
options: The neck
The forearm, preferred because it's most accurate
The lower extremity
The cuff can't be used, so an arterial line is required
questions.explanation: Special considerations include using the contralateral limb if an IV is in place, the lower extremity as an alternative site, and noting that forearm measurements can overestimate BP.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 62 (PDF p. 63)

questions.stem: How is medical air usually supplied in a hospital's central pipeline system?
options: A blend of O2 and nitrogen from separate cylinders
Compressed ambient air stored in a reservoir
H-cylinder banks of pure medical air only
Liquid air in vacuum-insulated tanks
questions.explanation: In the central supply, O2 is often stored as liquid in insulated tanks, N2O as compressed liquid, and medical air is often compressed ambient air held in a reservoir. Helium, nitrogen, and nitric oxide are usually in large cylinders.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 27 (PDF p. 14)

questions.stem: Which items belong to the 'Machine' step of the MS MAID room setup? Select 2.
options: Emergency drugs drawn up
A resuscitation bag/mask and an additional O2 cylinder
A rapid infuser and fluid warmer
A full machine check
A suction canister with Yankauer tip
An LMA and extra laryngoscope handle
questions.explanation: Machine: full check plus resuscitation bag/mask and an additional O2 cylinder. Suction is the S, the LMA and handle belong to Airway, the rapid infuser to IV, and emergency drugs to Drugs.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 3 (PDF p. 3)

questions.stem: During monitored anesthesia care, which parameters must be continually evaluated under ASA Standard II?
options: Oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature
Circulation only, since no airway device is placed
Ventilation and temperature only
Oxygenation and circulation only
questions.explanation: Standard II applies during ALL anesthetics: the patient's oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature shall be continually evaluated. Instructor note: minimum ETCO2, BP, temp, and SpO2.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 10 (PDF p. 10)

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes O2's two key temperatures?
options: -118.6 C is its boiling point at 1 atm; -183 C is its critical temperature
-183 C is the storage temperature of an E-cylinder
-183 C is its boiling point at 1 atm; -118.6 C is the highest temperature at which it can be liquid
Both are boiling points, at different cylinder pressures
questions.explanation: O2 boils at -183 C at 1 atm. Its critical temperature, -118.6 C, is the highest temperature at which it can exist as a liquid under pressure (instructor note). Bulk liquid O2 is stored below that critical temperature; E-cylinders hold compressed gas at room temperature.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slides 11, 12 (PDF p. 6)

questions.stem: During a field anesthetic, the O2 E-cylinder reads 950 psig and the N2O E-cylinder reads 745 psig. From the gauges alone, whose remaining contents can you estimate?
options: Only the N2O cylinder's
Both cylinders'
Neither cylinder's
Only the O2 cylinder's
questions.explanation: O2 is a compressed gas, so 950 psig is about half of 660 L, roughly 330 L. N2O stays at 745 psig while any liquid remains, so its gauge can't show contents; you'd have to weigh it.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slides 13, 14 (PDF p. 7)

questions.stem: PIP abruptly rises while plateau pressure is unchanged. What is the quickest first step to rule out tube-related causes?
options: Pass a suction catheter through the ETT
Deepen the anesthetic with volatile agent
Increase PEEP to recruit the lungs
Draw an arterial blood gas
questions.explanation: An isolated PIP rise means increased resistance or flow. Slide 32: airway secretions or a kinked tube can easily be ruled out with a suction catheter. Bronchospasm, foreign body, compression, and cuff herniation are the other causes on that list.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slides 26, 32 (PDF p. 26, 32)

questions.stem: The CO2 absorber is removed for replacement, and the case continues at 1 L/min fresh gas flow. What is the expected consequence?
options: Rebreathing of CO2 with rising ETCO2
Falling ETCO2 from reduced dead space
No change, since fresh gas flow washes out CO2
Compound A accumulation in the circuit
questions.explanation: The absorber is absolutely necessary in a low fresh gas flow technique. Without it, exhaled CO2 recirculates, so inspired and end-tidal CO2 rise. High fresh gas flows are what wash CO2 out of a circle without absorption.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 8 (PDF p. 4)

questions.stem: In a standard OR ventilation layout, where are the fresh air inflow and the exhaust port?
options: Both in the ceiling at opposite corners
Inflow on a wall near the floor; exhaust in the ceiling
Inflow above the anesthesia machine; exhaust at the scavenger
Inflow in the ceiling; exhaust on a wall about 6 inches above the floor
questions.explanation: The OR fresh air inflow port is in the ceiling, and the exhaust port is on an adjacent wall 6 inches above the floor.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 15 (PDF p. 8)

questions.stem: The capnogram baseline sits above zero. The absorbent is fresh, the unidirectional valves work, and FGF is high. What is the remaining explanation from the lecture?
options: Bronchospasm slowing exhalation
Increased metabolic CO2 production
Esophageal placement of the tube
The capnometer is calibrated incorrectly
questions.explanation: A baseline that doesn't return to zero means rebreathing (chemically exhausted absorber, malfunctioning valve, insufficient FGF) or an incorrectly calibrated device. With the rebreathing causes excluded, calibration is left. Increased production raises ETCO2, not the baseline.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 50 (PDF p. 51)

questions.stem: About how much vapor can be produced from a full 250 mL bottle of sevoflurane?
options: About 5 L
About 25 L
About 50 L
About 200 L
questions.explanation: The lecture's rule of thumb: 1 mL of liquid anesthetic makes about 200 mL of vapor. 250 mL x 200 mL = 50,000 mL, about 50 L.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 52 (PDF p. 26)

questions.stem: A small leak develops at the Y-piece, but no alarm has sounded yet. What is most likely to show it first?
options: A rise in the inspired O2 concentration reading
Subtle drops in PIP, exhaled volume, or ETCO2 before alarm limits
The low O2 supply pressure alarm sounding early
A rising PEEP trend triggering the high PEEP alarm
questions.explanation: Slide 33: a small leak or partial disconnect may be detected by subtle decreases in peak pressure, exhaled volume, or ETCO2 before alarm thresholds are reached. That's why trends matter more than waiting for the alarm.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 33 (PDF p. 33)

questions.stem: Tidal volume is increased from 450 to 650 mL. PIP and plateau both rise by similar amounts. What is the best interpretation?
options: A kinked endotracheal tube
A new decrease in lung compliance
An expected effect of the larger tidal volume
New bronchospasm
questions.explanation: The lecture: an increase in both PIP and plateau (gap roughly constant) can come from an increase in tidal volume OR decreased compliance. With a deliberate volume increase, the rise is expected. Bronchospasm and a kink raise PIP alone.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 26 (PDF p. 26)

questions.stem: A Tec 6 desflurane vaporizer is switched on and dialed to 6% right away, but the agent monitor shows no des. What is the MOST likely reason?
options: The vapor shut-off valve doesn't open until the vaporizer warms up
Des must first saturate wicks in the sump
The dial must be set above 6% before des flows
The differential pressure transducer requires high FGF to start
questions.explanation: Vapor circuit restrictor #1 is a shut-off that opens only when the vaporizer has warmed up and the dial is opened. Until the sump reaches operating temperature and pressure, no vapor is released. The Tec 6 has no wicks.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 62 (PDF p. 31)

questions.stem: On this tracing, which numbered point marks the end of ejection as the aortic valve closes?
options: Point 1
Point 3
Point 4
Point 5
questions.explanation: Point 4 is the dicrotic notch, the small dip on the downslope marking aortic valve closure and the start of diastole. Point 1 is the systolic upstroke (aortic valve opening), 3 the systolic decline, and 5 the diastolic runoff.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 72 (PDF p. 73)

questions.stem: During a stable anesthetic, FiO2 reads 60% and FeO2 reads 56%. What does the difference represent?
options: A circuit leak entraining room air
Rebreathing of expired gas
Normal O2 uptake by the patient
A malfunctioning O2 analyzer
questions.explanation: Instructor note: measure what's going in and what's coming out; expired is less than inspired. The difference reflects O2 taken up by the patient.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 11 (PDF p. 11)

questions.stem: A variable bypass vaporizer contains 250 mL of sevoflurane. Running 2% at 3 L/min fresh gas flow, about how long before it runs dry?
options: About 4 hours
About 7 hours
About 14 hours
About 42 hours
questions.explanation: Use mL/hr = vol% x FGF (L/min) x 3: 2 x 3 x 3 = 18 mL/hr. 250 mL divided by 18 mL/hr is about 14 hours. 42 hours forgets the factor of 3.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 52 (PDF p. 26)

questions.stem: A leak at which location would release gas at the LOWEST pressure?
options: The common gas outlet connection
The outlet of the second-stage O2 regulator
The O2 pipeline hose at the wall
The O2 cylinder yoke
questions.explanation: The low-pressure system (flowmeters to common gas outlet) runs slightly above atmospheric. The pipeline (about 50-55 psi) and second-stage regulator output (about 14-16 psi O2) are intermediate; the yoke is high pressure.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slides 33, 76 (PDF p. 17, 38)

questions.stem: The circuit O2 analyzer reads 60%. Which conclusion is valid?
options: Tissue oxygenation is adequate
Inspired O2 is 60%, but arterial oxygenation still has to be assessed separately
The circuit is connected and the patient is being ventilated
The patient's PaO2 must be adequate
questions.explanation: Adequate inspired O2 doesn't guarantee adequate arterial oxygenation, and inspired O2 alarms don't reliably detect circuit disconnection. The lecture says to pair inspired O2 monitoring with blood oxygenation monitoring, because circuit concentration alone doesn't measure PaO2 or tissue oxygenation.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 38 (PDF p. 38)

questions.stem: For the EASI derived 12-lead system, where are the LA and V electrodes placed?
options: LA on the lower sternum; V on the manubrium
LA on the manubrium; V on the lower sternum
LA on the left arm; V at the fifth intercostal space midclavicular
LA on the left mid-axillary line; V on the manubrium
questions.explanation: EASI provides a near-global 12-lead with unconventional placement: LA on the manubrium, V on the lower sternum, LL on the left mid-axillary line, RA on the right mid-axillary line. It's comparable to standard 12-lead for many cardiac diagnoses.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 57 (PDF p. 58)

questions.stem: Radial pulses are weak and the vessels small. What does the lecture say improves arterial cannulation success?
options: Performing an Allen test first
Using the smallest catheter blind
Choosing the brachial artery, which has collateral flow
Ultrasound with Doppler guidance
questions.explanation: Ultrasound (with Doppler) improves arterial cannulation when pulses are weak or vessels are small. The traditional Allen test hasn't been confirmed as reliable.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 66 (PDF p. 67)

questions.stem: Which cylinder safety relief device can reseal after venting excess pressure?
options: Spring-loaded relief valve
Fusible metal plug
Frangible metal disk
Bodok sealing washer
questions.explanation: The spring-loaded relief valve opens when pressure exceeds its threshold and closes again once pressure falls. A frangible disk breaks and a fusible plug melts, so both are one-time devices. The Bodok seal is a yoke washer, not a relief device.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 17 (PDF p. 9)

questions.stem: On a cold finger, SpO2 reads 97% but the plethysmograph is flat and noisy. How should the number be treated?
options: As accurate, since the displayed value is normal
As falsely low, so FiO2 should be increased
As unreliable until signal quality and perfusion are confirmed
As proof that tissue oxygenation is adequate
questions.explanation: Highlighted on slide 75: interpret the number together with signal quality, perfusion, clinical condition, and the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve. A poor waveform undercuts the number regardless of its value, and SpO2 never measures tissue oxygenation.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 75 (PDF p. 76)

questions.stem: Which are the three basic components of every direct laryngoscope? Select 3.
options: Handle
Cuff
Light source
Stylet
Blade
Video screen
questions.explanation: All DLs have three basic components: the handle, the blade, and the light source. A stylet belongs with the tube, and a screen belongs to video laryngoscopes.
questions.citation: Airway Equipment (McPherson): slide 11 (PDF p. 11)

questions.stem: Which statements correctly describe how the NIOSH limits are applied? Select 2.
options: Halogenated agent: no limit when scavenging is in use
Halogenated agent: ceiling concentration over a sampling period up to 1 hour
N2O: ceiling concentration over a sampling period up to 1 hour
N2O (sole agent): time-weighted average during anesthetic administration
N2O: applies only when combined with a halogenated agent
Halogenated agent: 8-hour time-weighted average
questions.explanation: Slide 10: N2O as the sole agent at no more than 25 ppm TWA during administration, and no worker exposed above 2 ppm of any halogenated agent. The halogenated value is a ceiling measured over a sampling period of up to one hour. Scavenging doesn't remove the limit.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 10 (PDF p. 5)
questions.supp: The one-hour ceiling sampling definition and the combined-use value (0.5 ppm halogenated when used with N2O) come from NIOSH's 1977 recommendation; slide 10 lists only 2 ppm and 25 ppm.

questions.stem: Which components make up an infrared gas analyzer? Select 3.
options: Infrared source
Optical path
Polarographic electrode
Galvanic fuel cell
Detector and signal processor
Magnetic field generator
questions.explanation: IR analyzers contain an infrared source, gas sampler, optical path, detector, and signal processor. Magnetic fields belong to paramagnetic O2 analyzers, and fuel cells and electrodes to galvanic and polarographic O2 sensors.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 40 (PDF p. 40)

questions.stem: A zone valve is closed during a fire in the next OR suite, cutting pipeline O2 to your room. What is the FIRST action?
options: Rely on the O2 flush to maintain ventilation
Open the machine's O2 E-cylinder
Switch to the auxiliary O2 flowmeter
Reopen the zone valve to restore pipeline O2
questions.explanation: Zone valves isolate areas for maintenance or emergencies, so pipeline O2 is gone. The backup cylinder supplies the machine through the first-stage regulator. The auxiliary flowmeter and flush draw from the same O2 supply, and reopening the valve would defeat the isolation.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slides 28, 33 (PDF p. 14, 17)

questions.stem: Which sequence traces waste gas from the breathing circuit to disposal?
options: Scavenging interface, relief valve, conducting tubing, disposal line
Conducting tubing, relief valve, disposal line, scavenging interface
Relief valve, scavenging interface, conducting tubing, disposal line
Relief valve, conducting tubing, scavenging interface, disposal line
questions.explanation: The four parts in order: (1) a relief valve where gas leaves the circuit (APL or ventilator relief valve), (2) conducting tubing to the interface, (3) the scavenging interface, and (4) a disposal line to the vacuum or ventilation system.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slides 18, 19 (PDF p. 9, 10)

questions.stem: According to closed-claims data in the lecture, what proportion of claims involve errors in judgment?
options: About 1%
About 10%
About 25%
More than 65%
questions.explanation: More than 65% of claims involve errors in judgment (failure to recognize or treat problems, poor planning, cognitive bias, production pressure, lack of vigilance). About 1% of claims (1990-2011) were equipment mishaps.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 7 (PDF p. 7)

questions.stem: A Tec 6 desflurane vaporizer is switched on and dialed to 6% right away, but the agent monitor shows no des. What is the MOST likely reason?
options: The vapor shut-off valve doesn't open until the vaporizer warms up
The dial must be set above 6% before des flows
Des must first saturate wicks in the sump
The differential pressure transducer requires high FGF to start
questions.explanation: Vapor circuit restrictor #1 is a shut-off that opens only when the vaporizer has warmed up and the dial is opened. Until the sump reaches operating temperature and pressure, no vapor is released. The Tec 6 has no wicks.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 62 (PDF p. 31)

questions.stem: Sodium bicarbonate is given for metabolic acidosis. ETCO2 rises from 36 to 45 mmHg, then drifts back over several minutes. What is the best response?
options: Change the CO2 absorbent immediately
Double minute ventilation until ETCO2 falls below 35
Recognize it as a transient expected rise and trend it
Treat it as malignant hyperthermia
questions.explanation: Transient ETCO2 increases occur after bicarbonate administration, tourniquet release, and aortic unclamping. A rise that settles on its own is expected. MH causes a sustained, progressive rise.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 41 (PDF p. 41)

questions.stem: The breathing circuit disconnects at the Y-piece. Can you rely on the inspired O2 analyzer to alarm?
options: Yes; FiO2 drops to 21% immediately
Yes; the analyzer senses loss of expired O2
No; inspired O2 alarms don't reliably detect circuit disconnection
No; the analyzer only works during spontaneous ventilation
questions.explanation: Slide 38: inspired O2 alarms do not reliably detect circuit disconnection, because the inspired limb can keep reading the delivered O2. Disconnect detection relies on low PIP, low exhaled volume, and low ETCO2.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 38 (PDF p. 38)

questions.stem: Late in a case, there's diffuse oozing from the surgical field. Platelet count was normal, and core temperature is 34.4 C. What should be addressed first?
options: Deeper anesthesia to reduce BP
Active warming, since hypothermia impairs coagulation
Additional platelet transfusion
Surgical exploration for a single bleeding vessel
questions.explanation: Perioperative hypothermia impairs coagulation (the instructor's note: low temp is bad for coagulation, wounds, and drug function). With a normal platelet count and a core temperature of 34.4 C, correcting temperature is the first step.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 84 (PDF p. 85)

questions.stem: The O2 pipeline is found to be contaminated with nitrogen during a case. What is the correct response?
options: Open the O2 cylinder and leave the pipeline connected
Increase the O2 flowmeter setting
Switch to the auxiliary O2 flowmeter
Open the O2 cylinder AND disconnect the pipeline hose
questions.explanation: The machine preferentially uses pipeline gas (50-55 psi) over the cylinder's regulated ~45 psi, so opening the cylinder alone changes nothing. The pipeline must be disconnected so the cylinder supplies O2. More flow or the auxiliary flowmeter just delivers more contaminated gas.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slides 33, 46 (PDF p. 17, 23)

questions.stem: What determines the slope of the capnogram's expiratory upstroke (B to C)?
options: The sampling line's distance from the monitor
The FiO2 delivered during inspiration
The inspiratory flow rate set on the ventilator
How evenly the lungs ventilate and alveoli empty during expiration
questions.explanation: At point B, CO2-containing gas reaches the sampling site and the upstroke begins. The slope is determined by the evenness of expiratory ventilation and alveolar emptying, which is why obstruction produces a slow, sloped rise.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 44 (PDF p. 44)

questions.stem: A patient on FiO2 1.0 has an SpO2 of 100%. What does this tell you about PaO2?
options: Only that it's on the flat upper curve; PaO2 could be 100 or 500
That the PaO2 is about 100 mmHg, the normal value
That PaO2 rises in exact proportion to FiO2
That the PaO2 is about 500 mmHg on FiO2 1.0
questions.explanation: The oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve is sigmoid and flat at the top: once hemoglobin is fully saturated, higher PaO2 doesn't change SpO2. A reading of 100% can't tell you how much reserve exists; an ABG is needed.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 76 (PDF p. 77)

questions.stem: Why is a copper kettle vaporizer made of copper?
options: Copper prevents the agent from reacting with O2
Copper's heat conduction keeps agent temperature and vapor output stable
Copper catalyzes vaporization of the liquid agent
Copper allows the kettle to be concentration-calibrated
questions.explanation: The copper kettle has great heat conduction to maintain stable temperatures as vaporization cools the liquid, which keeps vapor pressure steady. It still isn't calibrated for concentration, so calculations are required.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 74 (PDF p. 37)

questions.stem: With a closed-reservoir interface, hospital suction is excessive AND the negative-pressure (pop-in) relief valve is stuck closed. What is the risk?
options: Negative pressure transmitted to the breathing circuit
Waste gas venting into the room through the pop-off valve
Positive pressure buildup transmitted to the breathing circuit
No effect, because the reservoir bag absorbs any suction
questions.explanation: The pop-in valve protects the circuit from excessive negative pressure by letting room air into the reservoir. If it can't open, the suction pulls on the breathing circuit itself. Positive-pressure buildup and venting through the pop-off are the vacuum-FAILURE findings.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 20 (PDF p. 10)

questions.stem: Which factors must be considered when interpreting oscillometric NIBP readings? Select 3.
options: Inspired O2 concentration
ETCO2 value
Motion and cardiac rhythm
Limb position relative to the heart
Pulse oximeter probe site
Cuff size
questions.explanation: Interpret NIBP values with cuff size, limb position, motion, rhythm, and perfusion in mind. Low flow, arterial stiffness, motion, arrhythmia, tubing leaks, and rapid deflation can impair reliability. FiO2, ETCO2, and probe site don't affect the reading.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slides 87, 90 (PDF p. 88, 91)

questions.stem: Hospital vacuum to a closed interface fails, and the positive-pressure (pop-off) relief valve is stuck closed. What is the main danger?
options: Negative pressure pulling on the breathing circuit
Collapse of the interface reservoir bag
Pressure buildup transmitted back to the breathing circuit
Room air being entrained into the circuit
questions.explanation: With vacuum failure, waste gas accumulates and pressure builds in the reservoir; normally the pop-off vents it into the room. If that valve can't open, the pressure has nowhere to go but back toward the breathing circuit, risking barotrauma. Negative pressure and bag collapse come from EXCESSIVE suction.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 20 (PDF p. 10)

questions.stem: Which O2 analyzer performance targets does the lecture give? Select 2.
options: Reliable detection of circuit disconnection
Response time of about 2-10 seconds
Accuracy of about plus or minus 2% of the actual O2 level
Response time of about 1 minute
Calibration once a month
Accuracy of about plus or minus 10%
questions.explanation: Performance targets include a response time of about 2-10 seconds and accuracy of about plus or minus 2% of the actual O2 level. Galvanic sensors are calibrated daily, and inspired O2 alarms don't reliably detect disconnection.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 36 (PDF p. 36)

questions.stem: Why print a baseline ECG strip before induction?
options: Because ST monitoring can't be turned on until after induction
So intraoperative ST changes can be compared with the patient's own baseline
To calibrate the monitor's heart rate counter
To satisfy the ASA requirement for a pre-op 12-lead
questions.explanation: The lecture lists printing a baseline strip before induction and turning ST monitoring on. Fingerprinting depends on knowing the patient's baseline: if changes are already present in III and aVF, those are the leads to prioritize and compare against.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slides 57, 58 (PDF p. 58, 59)

questions.stem: The sevoflurane dial is turned from 1% to 3%. How does the splitting ratio (bypass flow to chamber flow) change?
options: It stays the same; only the chamber temperature changes
It decreases, as more fresh gas enters the vaporizing chamber
It increases, as more fresh gas bypasses the chamber
It stays the same; only total fresh gas flow changes
questions.explanation: The concentration control dial adjusts valves to direct more or less fresh gas into the vaporizing chamber. A higher setting sends more flow through the chamber to deliver a greater share of saturated vapor, so the bypass-to-chamber ratio falls.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slides 53, 54 (PDF p. 27)

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the scavenging interface?
options: Shield the breathing circuit from excess positive or negative disposal pressure
Filter anesthetic agents out of waste gas before it reaches disposal
Measure waste gas concentrations to document NIOSH compliance
Return unused anesthetic agent to the vaporizer for reuse
questions.explanation: The scavenging interface is a safety mechanism, with relief valves (closed type) or open ports (open type), interposed between the breathing circuit and the hospital vacuum or ventilation system. Its job is to keep the disposal system from exerting excessive high or low pressure on the circuit.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 20 (PDF p. 10)

questions.stem: Head repositioning changes the capnogram to this pattern. Before anything else, what should you do?
options: Give a bronchodilator for bronchospasm
Increase the ventilator rate to raise ETCO2
Replace the sampling line
Check ETT position and cuff, and confirm ventilation
questions.explanation: Small irregular waves that no longer reach a plateau match slide 46's decreasing-ETCO2 causes: cuff leak, tube in the hypopharynx, or partial obstruction. After head movement, tube position is the first thing to verify. Bronchospasm gives a shark fin, and a sampling problem wouldn't depend on the head turning.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 46 (PDF p. 47)

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly traces N2O from the pipeline to its flowmeter?
options: Fail-safe valve, pipeline inlet check valve, flow control valve, second-stage regulator, flowmeter
Pipeline inlet check valve, second-stage N2O regulator, flowmeter, fail-safe valve, flow control valve
Pipeline inlet check valve, flow control valve, fail-safe valve, flowmeter, second-stage regulator
Pipeline inlet check valve, fail-safe valve, second-stage N2O regulator, flow control valve, flowmeter
questions.explanation: On the machine roadmap, N2O pipeline gas passes the inlet check valve, then the fail-safe (A), then the second-stage N2O regulator (C), then the flow control (needle) valve and flowmeter. The fail-safe sits upstream so it can cut N2O before it reaches the flow controls.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slides 5, 31, 33, 34 (PDF p. 3, 16, 17)

questions.stem: After every position change, which patient check does the lecture emphasize?
options: Cycle the NIBP every minute for 10 minutes
Arms secured, head midline, no pressure points
Recalibrate the O2 analyzer to room air
Reprint a baseline ECG strip for comparison
questions.explanation: Patient checks: arms secured, head midline, body parts secured with position changes, and surgical equipment and instruments off pressure points or the airway and lines. Also: eyes taped, invasive lines secure, and IVs functional, not infiltrated.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 54 (PDF p. 55)

questions.stem: A sedated patient's obstruction seems to be mainly at the level of the soft palate. Which adjunct is better suited to relieve it?
options: Face mask with higher fresh gas flow to stent it open
Chin lift alone, without adding any airway adjunct
OPA, which lifts the tongue off the posterior pharynx
NPA, which passes behind the soft palate to the hypopharynx
questions.explanation: The tongue and soft palate are the two main sources of obstruction. An NPA passes through the nasopharynx behind the soft palate and lies in the hypopharynx, and awake or sedated patients tolerate it better. The OPA's job is lifting the tongue.
questions.citation: Airway Equipment (McPherson): slides 3, 5, 6 (PDF p. 3, 5, 6)

questions.stem: An O2 E-cylinder's gauge reads 0 psig. How much gas is inside?
options: About 30 L, since gauges read low when nearly empty
None; 0 psig means a complete vacuum
About 5 L of O2 at atmospheric pressure
About 660 L, because the gauge has failed
questions.explanation: Gauge pressure is pressure ABOVE atmospheric (Pg = Pabs - Patm). At 0 psig, the cylinder is at 14.7 psia, so its 5 L internal volume still holds about 5 L of gas at atmospheric pressure. It's unusable, but not a vacuum.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 12 (PDF p. 6)

questions.stem: Which conditions raise ETCO2 through hypoventilation? Select 3.
options: Residual neuromuscular blockade in a spontaneously breathing patient
CO2 insufflation for laparoscopy
CNS depression
Metabolic alkalosis in a spontaneously breathing patient
Pain and light anesthesia causing tachypnea
Fever raising metabolic CO2 production
questions.explanation: Box 18.1 lists COPD, neuromuscular paralysis or dysfunction, CNS depression, metabolic alkalosis (if spontaneously breathing), and medication effects under hypoventilation. Fever raises production, laparoscopy raises delivery, and pain causes HYPERventilation.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 43 (PDF p. 43)

questions.stem: Which O2 analyzer detects a pressure change in the sample line produced by O2's attraction to switched magnetic fields?
options: Galvanic
Paramagnetic
Polarographic
Infrared
questions.explanation: Paramagnetic analyzers exploit O2's attraction to magnetic energy, detecting sample pressure changes in switched magnetic fields. Galvanic and polarographic sensors generate current from O2 reactions; infrared measures CO2, N2O, and agents.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 35 (PDF p. 35)

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the direct laryngoscope blade?
options: Delivering O2 to the glottis during intubation
Guiding the tube through the vocal cords like a stylet
Creating an axis of visualization to the larynx
Measuring the depth of the vallecula
questions.explanation: All direct laryngoscopes have a handle, blade, and light source; the blade creates an axis of visualization to the larynx. The Mac and Miller do this by indirect and direct lifting of the epiglottis.
questions.citation: Airway Equipment (McPherson): slide 11 (PDF p. 11)

questions.stem: The lecture separates human factors from external distractions. Which are HUMAN factors? Select 3.
options: Noise
Boredom
Interruptions
Sleep deprivation
Music
Fatigue
questions.explanation: Human factors: fatigue, sleep deprivation, circadian disruption, and boredom. External distractions: noise, music, temperature, and interruptions. Self-initiated distraction includes handheld device use.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 7 (PDF p. 7)

questions.stem: Which step in the soda lime reaction sequence takes place over the course of minutes?
options: Sodium and potassium carbonates reacting with calcium hydroxide
Carbonic acid reacting with NaOH and KOH
Indicator dye responding to the change in pH
CO2 combining with water to form carbonic acid
questions.explanation: NaOH and KOH act like catalysts, quickly forming sodium and potassium carbonates. Those carbonates then react over minutes with calcium hydroxide to form calcium carbonate and water, regenerating NaOH and KOH.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 2 (PDF p. 1)

questions.stem: Per the instructor's notes, how many ECG views does a five-cable system give compared with a three-cable system?
options: Six views vs two views
Three views vs one view
Twelve views vs three views
Five views vs three views
questions.explanation: Instructor note: a 5-cable system gets 6 views, while a 3-cable system gets 2 views. The three-cable configuration (MCL5 + aVF) has limited sensitivity.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 57 (PDF p. 58)

questions.stem: This capnogram appears midway through a laparoscopy under controlled ventilation. What is the best response?
options: Assess NM blockade and redose the relaxant if indicated
Increase fresh gas flow to clear rebreathing
Replace the CO2 absorbent in the canister
Check the ETT cuff for a leak around the tube
questions.explanation: The dips in the plateau are curare clefts: spontaneous inspiratory effort out of sync with the ventilator. Instructor note: the patient is breathing spontaneously, so consider more paralytic, guided by quantitative NM monitoring. Rebreathing raises the baseline, and a cuff leak slopes or shrinks the waveform.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slides 15, 47 (PDF p. 15, 48)

questions.stem: Which statements about how waste gas is disposed of are correct? Select 2.
options: Passive disposal is standard in modern main ORs
Wall suction is preferred over a dedicated system
OR ventilation used for passive disposal must be nonrecirculating and meet NFPA-99
A separate, dedicated vacuum system for WAGs is preferred
Recirculating OR ventilation is acceptable for passive disposal
Passive through-the-wall disposal is an active route
questions.explanation: Active routes are wall suction or a dedicated evacuation system, and a separate dedicated WAG vacuum is preferable. When OR ventilation is used for passive disposal, it must be nonrecirculating and meet NFPA-99 and Facility Guidelines Institute requirements. Instructor note: passive disposal is seen more in makeshift ORs.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 21 (PDF p. 11)

questions.stem: Which situations call for measuring BP more often than every 5 minutes? Select 2.
options: Any patient with a correctly sized cuff
A stable ASA 1 patient during maintenance
A patient with an arterial line already in place
A stable MAC case with unchanged vital signs
During induction of anesthesia
A patient with ischemic heart disease and limited reserve
questions.explanation: Higher frequency (every 1-5 minutes) during induction reflects cardiac depressant and vasodilatory drug effects and unpredictable responses. It's also needed in patients with limited reserve, such as ischemic heart disease or high perioperative MI risk. For most stable cases, every 3-5 minutes is adequate.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 60 (PDF p. 61)

questions.stem: Tidal volume is increased from 450 to 650 mL. PIP and plateau both rise by similar amounts. What is the best interpretation?
options: New bronchospasm
An expected effect of the larger tidal volume
A new decrease in lung compliance
A kinked endotracheal tube
questions.explanation: The lecture: an increase in both PIP and plateau (gap roughly constant) can come from an increase in tidal volume OR decreased compliance. With a deliberate volume increase, the rise is expected. Bronchospasm and a kink raise PIP alone.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 26 (PDF p. 26)

questions.stem: During the morning check, the O2 cylinder is found open and pipeline pressure reads 42 psig. Over the first case, the cylinder gauge steadily falls. What is the best action?
options: Increase O2 flowmeter settings to draw more from the pipeline
Close the cylinder to keep it as backup and report the low pipeline pressure
Leave the cylinder open, since it is supplementing a weak pipeline
Switch to the auxiliary O2 flowmeter to spare the cylinder
questions.explanation: The machine draws from whichever source is at higher pressure. Pipeline normally runs 50-55 psi, above the cylinder's regulated ~45 psi. At 42 psig the open cylinder takes over and silently empties, leaving no backup. The auxiliary flowmeter draws from the same O2 supply.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 33 (PDF p. 17)

questions.stem: If this arterial line system became underdamped, which numbered point would be most exaggerated?
options: Point 2
Point 4
Point 5
Point 6
questions.explanation: Underdamping overestimates systolic pressure by 15-30 mmHg and amplifies artifacts, so the systolic peak (point 2) is overshot. Point 4 is the dicrotic notch, 5 the diastolic runoff, and 6 the end-diastolic pressure.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slides 69, 72 (PDF p. 70, 73)

questions.stem: A continuous flush device runs at 3 mL/hr on a neonate's arterial line. About how much fluid does it deliver over 24 hours?
options: About 24 mL
About 48 mL
About 72 mL
About 144 mL
questions.explanation: 3 mL/hr x 24 hr = 72 mL, from the flush alone. Continuous-flush devices typically infuse about 3-6 mL/hr, and the lecture notes this volume can matter in neonates.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 69 (PDF p. 70)

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly traces O2 from a machine E-cylinder to the common gas outlet?
options: Yoke check valve, first-stage regulator, flow control valve, second-stage regulator, vaporizer, flowmeter, outlet check valve
Yoke check valve, second-stage regulator, first-stage regulator, flowmeter, flow control valve, vaporizer, outlet check valve
First-stage regulator, yoke check valve, flow control valve, second-stage regulator, vaporizer, flowmeter, outlet check valve
Yoke check valve, first-stage regulator, second-stage regulator, flow control valve, flowmeter, vaporizer, outlet check valve
questions.explanation: High-pressure: yoke (with check valve), cylinder gauge, first-stage regulator. Intermediate: second-stage regulator (plus fail-safe and flush branches) up to the flow control valves. Low-pressure: flowmeters, then vaporizers, then the outlet check valve (if present) and common gas outlet.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slides 5, 22, 24, 33, 39, 49 (PDF p. 3, 11, 12, 17, 20, 25)

questions.stem: Mid-case, the N2O pipeline hose disconnects while O2 supply stays normal. What happens?
options: Both gases stop until the N2O pressure alarm is reset
N2O flow stops; O2 continues, and the fail-safe isn't involved
The fail-safe closes and cuts off O2 flow
O2 flow drops proportionally to keep the ratio constant
questions.explanation: The fail-safe responds only to falling O2 supply PRESSURE; it never shuts off O2 and isn't triggered by N2O loss. Losing N2O simply stops N2O delivery, which can lighten the anesthetic. Expired gas analysis would show N2O falling.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slides 26, 34 (PDF p. 13, 17)

questions.stem: For most stable cases, which NIBP interval does the lecture describe as adequate?
options: Every 3 to 5 minutes
Every 15 minutes
Every 1 minute throughout
Every 10 minutes
questions.explanation: A noninvasive BP measurement every 3 to 5 minutes is adequate in most cases, with technique and frequency set by patient condition and procedure. The standard is at least every 5 minutes.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 60 (PDF p. 61)

questions.stem: After a tipped vaporizer is drained, why does the fix include running it at the highest setting with high FGF for about 30 minutes?
options: To vaporize liquid agent left in the bypass chamber
To recalibrate the bimetallic strip
To test the interlock mechanism
To warm the vaporizer back to room temperature
questions.explanation: Tipping sends liquid agent into the bypass chamber, raising output. Draining removes the sump liquid; running high FGF at the highest setting clears residual liquid from the bypass, and refilling waits until expired gas analysis no longer detects agent.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 71 (PDF p. 36)

questions.stem: ETCO2 keeps rising despite doubling minute ventilation. The absorbent is fresh, inspired CO2 is zero, and the patient is tachycardic. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: Absorption of insufflated CO2 during laparoscopy
Rebreathing from an incompetent expiratory valve
Increased CO2 production, as in malignant hyperthermia
Hypoventilation from a ventilator leak
questions.explanation: Zero inspired CO2 rules out rebreathing, and doubled ventilation rules out simple hypoventilation. CO2 rising faster than you can blow it off points to increased production, and MH leads Box 18.1's list. With no insufflation described, laparoscopy doesn't fit.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slides 42, 43 (PDF p. 42, 43)

questions.stem: After a vaporizer is carried to another OR and remounted, expired sevoflurane reads 5% with the dial at 2%. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: A failed temperature compensation valve lowering output
A loose filler cap leaking agent
Liquid agent in the bypass chamber from tipping
The pumping effect from spontaneous ventilation
questions.explanation: Agent analysis catches vaporizer overdose. A vaporizer moved outside transport mode can tip, sending liquid into the bypass and raising output above the dial. A stuck compensation valve during cooling LOWERS output, a loose cap leaks agent out, and pumping is driven by positive pressure ventilation and flushing.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slides 42, 71 (PDF p. 21, 36); Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 42 (PDF p. 42)

questions.stem: Which figures about the environmental impact of inhaled anesthetics match the lecture? Select 3.
options: About 10% of total US greenhouse gases
About 1% of total US greenhouse gases
Up to 5% of a hospital's greenhouse gases
Less than 5% of a surgical procedure's carbon footprint
More than one-third of an average surgical procedure's carbon footprint
About half of a hospital's greenhouse gases
questions.explanation: Inhaled anesthetics account for more than one-third of an average procedure's carbon footprint, up to 5% of a hospital's greenhouse gases, and an estimated 1% of total US greenhouse gases.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 22 (PDF p. 11)

questions.stem: The vacuum on an open-reservoir interface is turned up far above what's needed. What is the effect on the breathing circuit?
options: Waste gas spills into the room through the open ports
Negative pressure pulls gas out of the breathing circuit
The reservoir bag collapses and the pop-in valve opens
Nothing significant; room air is drawn in through the open ports
questions.explanation: The open interface is valveless, and its relief ports are open to atmosphere, so excess suction just entrains room air through the ports instead of pulling on the circuit. Pop-in valves and reservoir bags belong to the closed interface, and spillage happens with too LITTLE vacuum.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 20 (PDF p. 10)

questions.stem: As bronchospasm worsens, how does point C on the capnogram change?
options: It moves to the left of point B
It becomes sharper as the upstroke steepens
It disappears as the baseline rises
It becomes more rounded as the upstroke slows
questions.explanation: Instructor note: C rounds out more with more obstruction. A slow B-to-C rise suggests COPD or acute obstruction (bronchospasm), producing the shark-fin pattern.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 45 (PDF p. 46)

questions.stem: In a patient with methemoglobinemia whose true SaO2 happens to be 85%, what SpO2 does a standard oximeter most likely show?
options: About 70%, underestimating saturation
About 99%, because MetHb reads as oxyhemoglobin
About 95%, overestimating saturation
About 85%, near the true value
questions.explanation: MetHb absorbs red and infrared light about equally, which the oximeter reads as about 85%. When the true saturation happens to be near 85%, the displayed value lands close to it. Above that point SpO2 underestimates, and below it SpO2 overestimates.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 75 (PDF p. 76)
questions.disc: Slide 75 places the crossover at 70%. Standard references (e.g., OpenAnesthesia) use 85%, matching the slide's own 1:1 = about 85% point. This question uses 85%.

questions.stem: What serves as the reserve O2 supply for a hospital whose main source is a bulk liquid O2 tank?
options: H-cylinder banks connected by manifolds
The auxiliary O2 flowmeters
The E-cylinders on each anesthesia machine
Compressed ambient air reservoirs
questions.explanation: O2 is stored as refrigerated liquid in vacuum-insulated tanks or as compressed gas in H-cylinder banks connected by manifolds, with portable refillable E-cylinders for transport and machine backup. H-cylinders are the hospital reservoir (instructor note).
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 11 (PDF p. 6)

questions.stem: A leak in the ventilator's bellows reduces the tidal volume actually delivered. How is ETCO2 likely to change?
options: No change, since the circuit is still sealed
Decrease, from increased dead space
Increase, from hypoventilation
Decrease, from dilution with room air
