questions.explanation: Box 18.1 lists ventilator leak among equipment causes of INCREASED ETCO2: less delivered volume means less CO2 eliminated. Circuit or ETT leaks that entrain room air around the sample are the ones listed under decreased ETCO2.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 43 (PDF p. 43)

questions.stem: During mask induction, vomitus appears inside the clear face mask. Which room setup item is essential at this moment?
options: A backup laryngoscope handle and blade
A spare O2 E-cylinder on the machine
A primed rapid infuser
Suction that is on, working, and within reach
questions.explanation: The clear mask lets you see vomitus, blood, and secretions, and suction is the S in MS MAID: canister, tubing, Yankauer, on and working, within reach. Backup airway gear and O2 matter too, but clearing the airway comes first.
questions.citation: Airway Equipment (McPherson): slide 4 (PDF p. 4); Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 3 (PDF p. 3)

questions.stem: In pediatric anesthesia, which monitor is more sensitive for detecting an unrecognized mainstem intubation?
options: NIBP
Pulse oximetry
Capnography
Temperature
questions.explanation: The lecture notes that pulse oximetry can be more sensitive than capnography for unrecognized mainstem (endobronchial) intubation in pediatric anesthesia, since one-lung ventilation affects oxygenation before ETCO2 changes much.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 78 (PDF p. 79)

questions.stem: During spontaneous ventilation with 5 L/min fresh gas flow, the APL valve is left fully closed. What happens?
options: The scavenger's negative-pressure relief valve opens to empty the circuit
Gas can't leave the circuit, so circuit pressure and the bag build up
Waste gas diverts to the ventilator relief valve
Excess gas vents through the CO2 absorber
questions.explanation: During spontaneous or assisted ventilation, the APL valve is the outlet for waste gas, and more than 5 L/min can exit through it depending on fresh gas flow. With it closed, incoming gas has nowhere to go, so circuit pressure rises (barotrauma risk). The ventilator relief valve is only in circuit during mechanical ventilation.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slides 11, 19 (PDF p. 6, 10)

questions.stem: During mechanical ventilation, the ventilator's disconnect alarm volume has been turned off. Which ASA requirement does this violate?
options: A disconnect-detecting device with an audible alarm must be continuous
Pulse oximetry must use a variable-pitch audible tone
NIBP must be cycled at least every 3 minutes throughout
ETCO2 must be monitored only until the incision is made
questions.explanation: When ventilation is controlled by a mechanical ventilator, a device capable of detecting disconnection must be in continuous use, and it must give an audible signal when its alarm threshold is exceeded. ETCO2 is monitored until removal or transfer, and BP is at least every 5 minutes.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 92 (PDF p. 93)

questions.stem: Which numbered component supplies N2O at about 26-38 psi to the N2O flow control valve?
options: Component 1
Component 2
Component 3
Component 4
questions.explanation: Component 3 is the second-stage N2O pressure regulator (about 26-38 psi). Component 2 is the second-stage O2 regulator (about 14-16 psi), 1 is the fail-safe upstream of it, and 4 is the pressure relief valve.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slides 5, 33 (PDF p. 3, 17)

questions.stem: What do Korotkoff sounds estimate during manual BP measurement?
options: Systolic and diastolic pressure
Mean arterial pressure only
Systolic pressure only
Pulse pressure only
questions.explanation: Palpation estimates systolic pressure from the return of the pulse during cuff deflation; Korotkoff sounds estimate systolic and diastolic pressure. Oscillometric devices associate MAP with maximal oscillation.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 86 (PDF p. 87)

questions.stem: Which setup step directly prevents the air embolism complication of pressurized arterial line flushing?
options: Using the shortest possible catheter
Leveling the transducer to the right atrium
Zeroing the transducer to atmosphere
Removing all air from the flush bag and tubing before use
questions.explanation: The lecture lists air embolism from pressurized flushing as a complication, and air bubbles also degrade waveform fidelity. De-airing the flush bag and tubing addresses both. Leveling and zeroing affect accuracy, not embolism risk.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 69 (PDF p. 70)

questions.stem: At the end of a long case, the patient is 34.6 C. Which effects of hypothermia are relevant as you plan emergence? Select 2.
options: Lower bleeding risk
Altered drug metabolism prolonging drug effects
Improved wound healing
Faster recovery from neuromuscular blockade
Reduced O2 consumption if shivering starts
Impaired coagulation
questions.explanation: Hypothermia increases shivering, cardiac work, and O2 consumption; impairs coagulation; alters drug metabolism; and is linked to wound infection. Slower metabolism prolongs drug effects, so confirm NMB recovery with quantitative monitoring. Instructor note: low temp is bad for coagulation, wounds, and drug function.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 84 (PDF p. 85)

questions.stem: During ventilation of a patient with long-standing lung disease, this pressure-volume loop appears. What does it MOST likely show?
options: A leak in the breathing circuit
Increased inspiratory resistance from a kinked ETT
Abnormally increased compliance, as in emphysema
Decreased compliance from pneumothorax
questions.explanation: The loop is tall and steep, hugging the volume axis: large volume for little pressure, the lecture's pattern for abnormally increased compliance (emphysema). Decreased compliance shifts toward the pressure axis, a leak leaves the loop open, and a kink bows the inspiratory limb.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slides 28, 29 (PDF p. 28, 29)

questions.stem: What purity does the lecture give for medical-grade O2?
questions.explanation: Medical-grade O2 is 99-99.5% pure. It's stored as compressed gas in H-cylinder banks and E-cylinders, or as refrigerated liquid below its critical temperature (-118.6 C).
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 11 (PDF p. 6)

questions.stem: The O2 flowmeter is set to 4 L/min with no air or N2O on, yet the inspired O2 analyzer reads 21%. Pipeline pressures are normal. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: Medical air is being delivered through the O2 pipeline
The proportioning system is limiting O2 flow
The galvanic sensor needs 100% O2 calibration
The fail-safe valve has closed the O2 line
questions.explanation: An O2 flowmeter delivering gas that reads 21% means the 'O2' line is carrying air, the same class of problem as the lecture's crossed-pipeline events. Pressure-based safeguards stay quiet because pressures are normal. Room-air calibration would make a working sensor read 21% in AIR, not in 100% O2.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 46 (PDF p. 23); Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 36 (PDF p. 36)

questions.stem: Which gas can't be detected by infrared spectroscopy, according to the lecture?
options: Xenon
Carbon dioxide
Sevoflurane
Nitrous oxide
questions.explanation: Infrared spectroscopy can't detect xenon. It does measure CO2 (near 4.3 microns), N2O, and the potent volatile agents.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 48 (PDF p. 49)

questions.stem: In the lecture's bulk liquid O2 diagram, about what pressure does the regulator deliver to the hospital pipeline?
options: About 745 psig
About 85 psig
About 14-16 psig
About 50 psig
questions.explanation: The bulk tank runs at about 85 psig with a safety relief valve. After vaporizing and superheating, a pressure regulator drops O2 to about 50 psig for the pipeline, consistent with the 50-55 psi pipeline pressure. 14-16 psi is the machine's second-stage O2 output.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 32 (PDF p. 16)

questions.stem: According to the lecture's analyzer table, which gas readings change with a breathing circuit disconnection? Select 3.
options: SpO2 on the pulse oximeter
O2
CO2
Arterial blood pressure
N2
Anesthetic agent
questions.explanation: The table lists disconnection as a CO2, O2, and agent analysis event. N2 appears with circuit leaks, cuff leaks, poor mask fit, gas delivery errors, and air embolism. SpO2 and BP aren't gas analyzer readings.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 42 (PDF p. 42)

questions.stem: In Diagram C, a leak develops in the leftmost (N2O) flowmeter tube. Which gas is lost through the leak?
options: N2O
O2
Air
All three equally
questions.explanation: In C (Drager: N2O, air, O2), gases flow toward the outlet on the right, with O2 entering last. A leak in the first tube loses N2O, while O2 downstream still reaches the outlet. That's why the lecture calls O2-last arrangements fail-safe.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 41 (PDF p. 21)

questions.stem: On the capnogram, what does phase D to E represent?
options: Anatomic dead space gas at the start of expiration
The alveolar plateau of expiration
The expiratory upstroke as alveolar gas arrives
Inspiration, with fresh gas entrained and CO2 falling to baseline
questions.explanation: D is ETCO2. As the patient begins to inspire, fresh gas is entrained and there's a steep downstroke (D to E) back to baseline. Unless rebreathing of CO2 occurs, the baseline approaches zero.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 44 (PDF p. 44)

questions.stem: During a sevoflurane/N2O anesthetic, room sampling shows sevoflurane 0.8 ppm and N2O 20 ppm TWA. How do these compare with NIOSH recommendations?
options: Sevo exceeds its combined-use limit; N2O is within limits
N2O exceeds its limit; sevo is within limits
Both are within limits
Both exceed their limits
questions.explanation: When a halogenated agent is used WITH N2O, its limit drops to 0.5 ppm, so sevo at 0.8 ppm exceeds it even though it would be under the 2 ppm limit for use alone. N2O's 25 ppm TWA isn't exceeded at 20 ppm.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 10 (PDF p. 5)
questions.supp: The 0.5 ppm combined-use limit comes from NIOSH's 1977 recommendation; slide 10 lists only 2 ppm and 25 ppm.

questions.stem: Which methods satisfy the ASA requirement for quantitative ETCO2 monitoring? Select 3.
options: Capnometry
Mass spectroscopy
Capnography
A colorimetric CO2 detector
Auscultation of breath sounds
Observation of chest rise
questions.explanation: Continual ETCO2 analysis must use a quantitative method such as capnography, capnometry, or mass spectroscopy. Colorimetric detectors are qualitative, and breath sounds and chest rise are clinical signs.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 92 (PDF p. 93)

questions.stem: During laser airway surgery, which elements complete the fire triad? Select 3.
options: Laser energy as the heat source
O2 or N2O as oxidizer
N2O as the fuel source
PVC endotracheal tube as fuel
Air as the ignition source
Saline in the cuff as fuel
questions.explanation: Same triad as the cylinder fire slide: oxidizer + fuel + heat. In the airway, a flammable PVC tube is fuel, O2 or N2O is the oxidizer, and the laser supplies heat (direct contact). Saline in the cuff protects it, and N2O is an oxidizer, not a fuel.
questions.citation: Airway Equipment (McPherson): slide 9 (PDF p. 9); Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 8 (PDF p. 4)

questions.stem: Which ECG lead does the lecture recommend monitoring for rhythm, including atrial arrhythmias?
options: Lead II
V3
V5
aVL
questions.explanation: Lead selection is guided by history and the pre-op 12-lead. Lead II is used for rhythm analysis (such as atrial arrhythmias), while V3, V4, and V5 are the most sensitive leads for ischemia.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 58 (PDF p. 59)

questions.stem: Per the instructor's notes, which items are checked on the anesthesia machine during the room sweep? Select 3.
options: Pipeline zone valve position
Absorbent color change and the ETCO2 waveform and number
ETCO2 line water trap
O2 flush flow rate in L/min
Bulk liquid O2 tank level
Vaporizer delivery and fill level
questions.explanation: Slide 24 notes: vaporizer (delivery, fill level), ETCO2 line water trap, and CO2 absorbent canister (color change, ETCO2 waveform and number). Bulk tank levels and zone valves are facility systems, not part of the machine sweep.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 24 (PDF p. 24)

questions.stem: Which lists the agents from LONGEST to shortest atmospheric lifetime?
options: Sevoflurane, isoflurane, desflurane, N2O
N2O, desflurane, isoflurane, sevoflurane
Desflurane, N2O, isoflurane, sevoflurane
N2O, isoflurane, desflurane, sevoflurane
questions.explanation: Atmospheric lifetimes: N2O up to 114 years, desflurane 14 years, isoflurane 3.2 years, sevoflurane 1.1 years.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 22 (PDF p. 11)

questions.stem: The lecture classifies some signs of bag-mask ventilation as clinical rather than objective. Which are the clinical signs? Select 2.
options: Chest movement
Exhaled tidal volume
Excessive gas leak
Waveform exhaled CO2
Sustained oxygen saturation
Peak airway pressure
questions.explanation: Mask ventilation is defined by clinical signs (chest movement, excessive gas leak) and objective measures (sustained SpO2, waveform exhaled CO2, peak airway pressure, exhaled tidal volume).
questions.citation: Airway Equipment (McPherson): slide 4 (PDF p. 4)

questions.stem: A machine has O2 positioned last in the flowmeter sequence. A crack develops in the O2 flowmeter tube itself. Is the patient protected from a hypoxic mixture?
options: Yes; O2-last placement protects against any flowmeter leak
Yes; the proportioning system increases O2 flow to compensate
Yes; the fail-safe valve detects the leak and stops N2O
No; O2 leaks from its own tube, so the O2-last design can't prevent it
questions.explanation: O2-last placement protects against leaks in UPSTREAM tubes. A leak in the O2 tube itself loses O2 regardless of position, and the lecture lists flowmeter cracks and leaks among causes of hypoxic mixtures. The fail-safe and proportioner sense pressure and flow settings, not leaks, so the inspired O2 analyzer is the safeguard.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slides 41, 48 (PDF p. 21, 24)

questions.stem: Which end-of-day habit best prevents CO2 absorbent desiccation?
options: Emptying the reservoir bag into the room
Turning off all fresh gas flows
Leaving the vaporizer at a low setting overnight
Leaving O2 at 10 L/min to keep the circuit clean
questions.explanation: High O2 flows over the absorbent during a weekend or after prolonged use desiccate it, which leads to CO production. Instructor note: at the end of the day turn flows off so you don't desiccate the absorbent.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 7 (PDF p. 4)

questions.stem: Which OR ventilation design are most ORs equipped with?
options: Recirculating, with filtered stale air mixed in
Recirculating, with at least 3 fresh exchanges per hour
Nonrecirculating, discarding all stale air
Passive, relying on door and window leaks
questions.explanation: Most ORs have a nonrecirculating system that pumps in fresh outside air and removes and discards all stale air, with 15 or more exchanges per hour recommended (instructor: this is how most ORs are set up). Recirculating systems exist but can carry anesthetic gases between rooms.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 16 (PDF p. 8)

questions.stem: The capnogram suddenly goes flat, the high peak pressure alarm sounds, and the bag can't be squeezed. What is the MOST likely problem?
options: Circuit disconnection at the Y-piece
Massive pulmonary embolism
Sampling line disconnection
Complete airway or tube obstruction
questions.explanation: Complete airway obstruction appears in Box 18.1 among equipment causes of decreased ETCO2, and HIGH pressure with no gas movement points to obstruction. A disconnection gives LOW pressure alarms, a sampling problem doesn't affect ventilation, and PE doesn't prevent bagging.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slides 33, 43 (PDF p. 33, 43)

questions.stem: Which indicator float designs does the lecture list for traditional flowmeters? Select 3.
options: Bourdon
Skirted
Bimetallic
Diaphragm
Ball
Plumb bob
questions.explanation: Indicator floats: skirted, plumb bob, nonrotating, and ball. Bimetallic strips are vaporizer temperature compensators, Bourdon tubes are pressure gauges, and diaphragms are in pressure regulators.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 42 (PDF p. 21)

questions.stem: A variable bypass vaporizer's temperature compensation valve sticks during a long case as the liquid agent cools. How will output compare with the dial?
options: Equal to the dial, because vapor pressure doesn't change with temperature
Lower than dialed
Higher than dialed
Equal to the dial, because the wicks compensate
questions.explanation: Vapor pressure is directly proportional to temperature, so cooling lowers the concentration leaving the chamber. Normally the bimetallic strip bends to increase chamber flow and compensate. If it's stuck, nothing corrects the drop, and output falls below the dial.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 56 (PDF p. 28)

questions.stem: Monday's first case uses desflurane with absorbent that dried out over the weekend. Which statements are correct? Select 2.
options: Compound A is the main risk with desflurane
ETCO2 monitoring detects carbon monoxide
Carbon monoxide can form in the absorbent
SpO2 will read falsely low and flag the problem
A standard pulse oximeter may read falsely high if COHb forms
Barium hydroxide lime would reduce CO formation
questions.explanation: Desiccated absorbent with des produces the most CO (des > enflurane > iso). Two-wavelength oximetry reads COHb like oxyhemoglobin, so SpO2 can look falsely reassuring (monitoring slide 75). Compound A is a sevoflurane problem, and Baralyme produces MORE CO than soda lime.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 7 (PDF p. 4); Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 75 (PDF p. 76)

questions.stem: A sevoflurane vaporizer is mistakenly filled with isoflurane and dialed to 2%. How will output compare with the dial?
options: Equal to the dial, because the splitting ratio is fixed
Higher than dialed, because iso's vapor pressure (240) exceeds sevo's (160)
Lower than dialed, because iso's vapor pressure is lower than sevo's
Equal to the dial, because temperature compensation corrects it
questions.explanation: The splitting ratio is calibrated to sevo's vapor pressure (160 mmHg), and ratios differ among agents based on vapor pressure. Iso's higher vapor pressure (240 mmHg) saturates chamber gas at a higher concentration, so output exceeds the dial. The lecture's intervention: always double-check bottle, key, and vaporizer.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slides 50, 54 (PDF p. 25, 27)

questions.stem: Only inspiratory flow is changed, from 30 to 60 L/min. PIP goes from 20 to 28 cmH2O while plateau stays at 16. What is the best interpretation?
options: A new decrease in lung compliance
An increase in tidal volume
An expected effect of higher inspiratory flow
New bronchospasm requiring treatment
questions.explanation: The lecture: an increase in PIP without a change in plateau signals increased airway resistance OR increased inspiratory gas flow rate. After a deliberate flow increase, the PIP rise is expected. Compliance or tidal volume changes raise plateau too.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 26 (PDF p. 26)

questions.stem: During preoxygenation, why does the lecture recommend head straps on the mask?
options: They deliver a higher FiO2 than holding the mask by hand
They keep the mask sealed hands-free while monitors and drugs are placed
They remove the need for a tight seal around the face
They protect against aspiration during preoxygenation
questions.explanation: The pre-induction slide: mask seal with FiO2 100% for 3-5 minutes or until expired O2 is at least 90%, and head straps keep the mask sealed hands-free so other monitors, drugs, and lines can be placed. Straps hold the seal; they don't raise FiO2 or protect against aspiration.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 91 (PDF p. 92)

questions.stem: For laser microlaryngoscopy with a laser-resistant tube, which gas choice best reduces ignition risk?
options: N2O with a small O2 fraction
Air/O2 at the lowest acceptable FiO2
O2/N2O to lower the O2 fraction
100% O2 to maximize safety margin
questions.explanation: Ignition depends on tube material, the concentration of O2 or N2O, and direct heat contact. N2O supports combustion like O2, so swapping O2 for N2O doesn't lower risk. Air with the lowest acceptable FiO2 reduces the oxidizer concentration.
questions.citation: Airway Equipment (McPherson): slide 9 (PDF p. 9)

questions.stem: What fills the headspace of the Tec 6 desflurane sump during operation?
options: Fresh gas saturated with desflurane at 1 atm
Heated O2 that picks up desflurane from wicks
100% desflurane vapor at about 2 atm (1500 mmHg)
A 21% desflurane mixture in carrier gas
questions.explanation: The sump heats liquid des to 39 C and pressurizes it to about 2 atm, acting as a reservoir of 100% des vapor. Fresh gas never enters the sump; vapor is injected into the fresh gas stream through restrictor valves.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slides 60, 61 (PDF p. 30, 31)

questions.stem: A machine's proportioning system links O2 and N2O. With no N2O running, O2 is turned to 0.2 L/min and air to 3 L/min. Will the proportioner prevent a low FiO2?
options: No; it links O2 to N2O, not to air
Yes; the fail-safe will stop air flow
No; proportioners only work at low total flows
Yes; it holds FiO2 above 25% for any gas mixture
questions.explanation: The lecture describes the proportioning system as linking O2 and N2O at the flow control valves so FiO2 stays above about 25% when N2O is used. Air isn't part of that link, and the fail-safe acts on O2 supply pressure, which is normal here. The O2 analyzer is the check.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 45 (PDF p. 23)

questions.stem: Which statements correctly describe how MAP is obtained? Select 2.
options: Both: measured directly by Korotkoff sounds
Both: the simple average of systolic and diastolic pressure
Oscillometric MAP: calculated from the area under the waveform
Invasive MAP: the point of maximal cuff oscillation
Oscillometric MAP: the point of maximal cuff oscillation
Invasive MAP: calculated from the area under the arterial waveform
questions.explanation: On an arterial waveform, MAP is the average pressure calculated from the total area under the curve. Oscillometric devices associate MAP with the maximal oscillation amplitude and estimate SBP and DBP by algorithm. MAP is not a simple average, since diastole is longer.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slides 72, 86 (PDF p. 73, 87)

questions.stem: ETCO2 has risen from 36 to 44 mmHg with unchanged ventilator settings, and the inspired CO2 baseline is still zero. Which cause is ruled out?
options: Absorption of insufflated CO2
Rebreathing
Increased CO2 production
Decreased elimination from hypoventilation
questions.explanation: Rebreathing (exhausted absorbent, bad valves, low FGF) shows up as a baseline that doesn't return to zero. A zero baseline rules it out and leaves increased production, increased delivery (laparoscopy), or decreased elimination.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slides 43, 50 (PDF p. 43, 51)

questions.stem: During prolonged low-flow positive pressure ventilation, which practices reduce the vaporizer pumping effect? Select 2.
options: Use the O2 flush frequently to clear the vaporizer
Avoid very low fresh gas flow when possible
Remove the outlet check valve to reduce back pressure
Keep the vaporizer adequately filled
Fill until bubbling stops to maximize liquid level
Run the vaporizer at its highest setting
questions.explanation: Pumping is worsened by PPV, O2 flush use, low FGF, and low liquid levels, and it's minimized by the outlet check valve between vaporizer and common gas outlet. Frequent flushing ADDS retrograde pressure, and filling until bubbling stops risks overfilling.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 72 (PDF p. 36)

questions.stem: Which ASA monitoring elements must be CONTINUOUS rather than intermittent? Select 2.
options: Temperature measurement at set intervals
Palpation of a peripheral pulse
NIBP measurement at set intervals
Auscultation of heart sounds by stethoscope
A ventilator disconnect-detecting device with audible alarm
ECG display
questions.explanation: The ECG must be continuously displayed, and during mechanical ventilation a disconnect-detecting device must be in continuous use. BP and HR are determined at least every 5 minutes, temperature when changes are expected, and palpation or auscultation are among the options for continual circulation assessment.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slides 13, 92 (PDF p. 13, 93)

questions.stem: A patient begins shivering vigorously in the PACU while still intubated. How is ETCO2 likely to change?
options: Decrease, from increased dead space
No change, since shivering doesn't affect CO2
Increase, from higher CO2 production
Decrease, from hyperventilation
questions.explanation: Increased skeletal muscle activity raises metabolic rate and CO2 production; Box 18.1 lists increased metabolic rate or skeletal muscle activity, and the ETCO2 changes table lists shivering. Shivering also raises O2 consumption.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slides 43, 51 (PDF p. 43, 52)

questions.stem: For a long case in an obese patient, which potent volatile agent has the lowest fat:blood solubility in the lecture's table?
options: Isoflurane (45)
Sevoflurane (48)
Desflurane (27)
Halothane (51)
questions.explanation: Fat:blood solubility: halothane 51, sevo 48, iso 45, des 27, N2O 2.3. Among the potent volatiles, des has the least fat solubility, so less agent accumulates in adipose tissue during long cases.
questions.citation: Medical Gas Systems in Anesthesia (Elmore): slide 50 (PDF p. 25)

questions.stem: Why does the indicator dye change color as the absorbent is used?
options: The granules heat up during neutralization
Water content in the granules rises
pH falls as hydroxides are converted to carbonates
CO2 binds directly to the dye molecules
questions.explanation: As carbonate forms from the hydroxide, pH becomes less alkaline, and the dye changes color (ethyl violet white to purple). Heat and water are also produced, but the dye responds to pH.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 4 (PDF p. 2)

questions.stem: A long sevoflurane anesthetic runs at 0.5 L/min fresh gas flow, and the absorbent canister is warm. Which change most directly reduces compound A production?
options: Let the absorbent dry out
Switch to barium hydroxide lime
Increase the sevoflurane concentration
Increase fresh gas flow
questions.explanation: Compound A is promoted by warmer, drier absorbent, higher agent concentration, and LOWER fresh gas flow. Raising FGF works against it. Drying the absorbent and raising agent concentration both increase compound A.
questions.citation: CO2 Absorbents and Scavenging (McPherson): slide 6 (PDF p. 3)

questions.stem: An adult-size cuff is placed on a small child's arm, covering most of the upper arm. How will readings be affected?
options: Falsely high, because the child's arm is below heart level
Falsely low, because the cuff is too large
Accurate, because larger cuffs are always safer
Falsely high, because the cuff is too large
questions.explanation: Cuff too small gives falsely high readings; cuff too large gives falsely low readings. Nothing in the stem suggests limb position is a factor.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 62 (PDF p. 63)

questions.stem: A pulmonary artery catheter is in place. How does PA blood temperature compare as a core temperature estimate?
options: It reflects skin temperature more than core
It lags behind rectal temperature
It's a strong estimate of central core temperature
It's unreliable during mechanical ventilation
questions.explanation: Core temperature can be estimated from several sites, and pulmonary artery blood temperature is also a strong estimate of central core temperature. Rectal temperature is the site that can lag during active cooling or rewarming.
questions.citation: Intraoperative Assessment, Monitoring & Data Interpretation (Stone): slide 81 (PDF p. 82)
